en.title: Google’s latest Search upgrade promises better answers to your most complicated questions
en.summary: Powered by Gemini 4 Hydrogen, Google's AI Mode is getting better at understanding complex queries, surfacing relevant links, and delivering richer visual responses.
en.body:
Google Search is getting better at understanding complicated questions, including those with multiple parts, highly specific requests, or confusing typos. The updates are coming via the company’s newly released Gemini 4 Hydrogen model, which Google claims is its “biggest model improvement to Search yet.”

While Google’s frontier models, Gemini 4 Carbon and Gemini 4 Argon, are best at deep reasoning for hard problems, Hydrogen is designed for fast execution across a variety of agentic workflows, or tasks in which an AI carries out multiple steps on its own, the company explained in an announcement.

The idea behind the model’s release is that using the most powerful model isn’t always needed — sometimes a faster, cheaper, and reasonably smart one will do. Google says Hydrogen completes tasks 2.5 times faster than Gemini 3.8 Flash, its previous fast model, but it’s still pretty smart, even beating the more powerful Gemini 4 Argon on one broad intelligence benchmark, the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index , at its default high thinking level.

In Search, Hydrogen brings several improvements, including a better understanding of user intent, the ability to offer more helpful links and visual responses, and better answers across the different languages supported by Google’s AI Mode.

In terms of intent, Google says Hydrogen can handle more nuanced and complicated questions more quickly. This means people can ask their questions in their natural train of thought, including those that have multiple parts or that include highly specific requests. Hydrogen is also better at navigating hard-to-understand typos, Google says. Because of its improvements and better ability to follow instructions and call the right tools, Hydrogen is able to more precisely address each part of a user’s question.

Its advanced reasoning also improves Search’s fan-out technique, which breaks down a single user’s prompt into multiple subqueries. This allows people to discover websites related to the query that they may have otherwise missed, the blog post explains.

The addition of Hydrogen to Search will also mean more images, structured responses, comparison tables, and custom tools will appear as visual responses to users’ queries in AI Mode.

Google also says Hydrogen can work on its own for everyday work in areas like writing code, running tests, or verifying code changes, or it can be paired with Carbon and Argon in workflows that combine several models.

The model offers four thinking levels: low, medium, high (default), and a new, extra-high tier (“xhigh”), all of which are designed to complete tasks faster with fewer output tokens.

On multi-step tasks like deep research, data analysis, and broad codebase navigation, Hydrogen ranks No. 5 on Agent Arena’s benchmarks, the company pointed out.

In addition to Search, Gemini 4 Hydrogen is coming to all tiers of Google’s AI Studio, the Gemini API, the Gemini App, and the paid AI Pro and Ultra subscribers in Google’s Antigravity development platform.

Google says the Hydrogen update is rolling out to all Search users globally.

en.title: Google rolls out Gemini 4 Hydrogen, finally replacing 3.8 Flash
en.summary: Gemini 4 Hydrogen isn't getting a slow, security-conscious release like Carbon and Argon.
en.body:
Google is continuing its elemental AI naming scheme with the new Gemini 4 Hydrogen . These names are less descriptive than the Pro/Flash monikers of earlier releases, but Hydrogen's purpose is clear: It replaces the faster, more economical Flash models most people in Google's ecosystem use.

With Google's recent Argon and Carbon releases, the rollout was staged and began with cybersecurity researchers. Even when general availability began, Google restricted access to users paying for its most expensive AI subscription. The limits for Hydrogen are much more relaxed, with access beginning immediately. This model has replaced Gemini 3.8 Flash across the company's products.

Google claims that Hydrogen represents a major improvement versus the previous Flash model. It runs in one of four thinking levels (low, medium, high, and the new xhigh), and even in high mode, it's 2.5 times faster than Flash 3.8. Plus, it reduces "fabricated claims" by more than 5x, according to Google's analysis. Users will also see gains in code generation, with Hydrogen more than tripling 3.8 Flash's score in Terminal-Bench. In some cases, Hydrogen even trades blows with Argon. It managed a score of 54 in the popular Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index with xhigh mode versus 50 for Argon.

en.title: iOS 27’s Find My app adds convenient feature I’ve long wished for
en.summary: iOS 27 is packed with new features, including several for the Find My app . One upgrade to Find My—custom sharing durations—grants a feature request I’ve had for years. more…
en.body:
iOS 27 is packed with new features, including several for the Find My app . One upgrade to Find My—custom sharing durations—grants a feature request I’ve had for years.

Apple’s Find My app is a great way to share your location with friends or family members on either permanent or a temporary basis.

But the “temporary” option just got a very welcome upgrade in iOS 27.

That’s because you can now set up location sharing in Find My for a custom duration. Per Apple :

users [now] have more control over how they share their location with friends and family using Find My, with new options to share for a custom duration — either for a number of minutes, hours, or days — or even set a date and time for when sharing will stop. This makes it easy for users to share their location while attending an event, or for a long weekend getaway with friends and family.

Until iOS 27, you could only choose from a very limited set of “temporary” options for sharing: for one hour, or until end of day. The only other option was “indefinitely.”

The main time I find myself adding new people to share my location with, I’m either traveling or they’re visiting me. On these occasions, the “one hour” and “until end of day” options never cut it.

So of course, I have to choose “indefinitely.” Then there’s the decision after the trip ends of either continuing to let location sharing happen, or ending sharing immediately (if I remember to). And the latter option has always felt a little awkward to me. I’d much rather schedule the sharing duration upfront.

And now with iOS 27 I can. When sharing location with someone, a new ‘Custom’ duration option allows choosing an end date and time, and/or manually setting a given number of days, hours, and minutes for sharing to continue.

It’s a great change, long overdue, and works perfectly for the scenarios Apple outlined.

Have you ever wished for custom sharing durations in Find My? Let us know in the comments.

en.title: Nectar launches an AI agent to automate creator discovery and outreach for brands
en.summary: Nectar's new AI agent automates influencer marketing, helping brands discover creators, manage outreach and partnerships, and track campaign results.
en.body:
Nectar , an AI-powered operating system for marketing, is launching a new AI agent designed to take a lot of the manual work out of influencer marketing, from finding the right creators to contacting them, managing partnerships, and tracking results.

Founded by sisters Misbah and Farah Uraizee, both former Meta employees, Nectar came out of stealth last year and uses AI agents to help brands manage social media, customer conversations, content moderation, creator partnerships, and competitor research.

Announced Thursday, its new “Creator Agent” can search for creators, check their content and brand partnerships, send personalized messages, coordinate collaborations, and monitor how campaigns perform. Instead of having marketing teams spend weeks scrolling through social media, building spreadsheets, and sending individual DMs, Nectar wants its agent to handle much of that work automatically.

Nectar joins other companies introducing agentic AI assistants designed to automate influencer outreach, including Aspire and GRIN . The launch also comes as more brands turn to creators to reach customers. U.S. spending on creator advertising is expected to reach $44 billion in 2026, according to the Interactive Advertising Bureau . As companies work with hundreds or even thousands of creators, keeping track of relationships and measuring results can get pretty difficult.

Nectar says its Creator Agent searches more than 300 million creator profiles to find potential partners, including smaller creators who may not yet have a large following but are gaining traction. The system analyzes videos to understand what creators post about, how their content fits a brand, and whether their previous partnerships are appropriate. It also checks brand safety by reviewing content in context rather than simply searching for specific keywords.

Nectar then creates ranked lists of recommendations and adds new matches as creators become more popular.

Once it finds a potential match, the agent can draft and send messages in a brand’s voice, create custom landing pages to collect creator information, and help manage contracts, product gifting, and shipping details. It also remembers previous conversations and interactions, so brands can keep track of relationships without relying on spreadsheets.

“Brands can share voice guidelines in any format, and Nectar picks up the rest from their history,” CEO Misbah Uraizee tells TechCrunch. “On top of that sits a set of proprietary guardrails that keep every draft on tone and in context. Nectar understands what is being said in a video, reads the tone of the conversation, and knows the difference between a quote post on X and a TikTok comment section. A brand should not sound identical in both, and with Nectar it doesn’t.”

Another feature looks for personal milestones in creators’ lives, such as an engagement, a new baby, or completing a marathon. The agent can then suggest a personalized message or gift, helping brands build relationships that feel less like one-off advertising deals.

Creator Agent is available today globally and covers Instagram creators and TikTokers.

The company plans to make the agent available through its Model Context Protocol (MCP), allowing teams to use it through AI assistants such as Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, and Copilot, as well as their own custom-built agents.

This past May, Nectar raised a $30 million Series A round led by Menlo Ventures and its Anthology Fund, which is a joint initiative launched with Anthropic.

He's placed himself indispensably at the center of the AI industry and famously had no succession plan at Nvidia. In fact, he's the only CEO Nvidia has ever had. L'état c'est moi. Then […]
en.body:
I was certain, until the story of Jensen Huang's second affair hit, that Huang was bulletproof. After all, why wouldn't he be? He's placed himself indispensably at the center of the AI industry and famously had no succession plan at Nvidia. In fact, he's the only CEO Nvidia has ever had. L'état c'est moi.

Then two stories were published nearly back to back on Wednesday: one alleging Huang had an affair with his subordinate Kimberly Powell, another that the board was meeting to consider his ouster. First thing Thursday morning, Nvidia announced Huang had resigned. One of the most powerful men in Silicon Valley was out.

Read the full story at The Verge.

en.title: United Airlines blocks AI agents from booking flights, citing cybersecurity risks
en.summary: The airline said it will not allow customers to use AI agents to book flights and manage reservations.
en.body:
Posted:

United Airlines said it will restrict access to AI agents seeking to book flights and manage reservations on their users’ behalf, citing a risk to cybersecurity and undermining federal regulations.

The airline is the latest American corporate giant to prevent customers from using AI agents and autonomous assistants to access their systems. The move comes as airlines and banks are struggling to differentiate between real customers and AI systems operating on their behalf, such as when users share their logins with their AI assistants. Sharing passwords with apps and assistants can create security risks if those credentials get leaked or exposed.

United warns that “sharing account credentials with personal, third-party, AI assistants can expose sensitive information, and actions taken by these tools may result in unintended purchases, account changes, or use of MileagePlus miles.”

The airline also warns of a risk of violating federal aviation rules, such as requiring that a human completes flight check-ins to acknowledge that their bags do not contain banned substances.

“As a result, United is taking steps to restrict access — directly within our digital platforms and indirectly via travel agencies and aggregators — to prohibit use by unauthorized, third-party personal AI agents or assistants,” the airline said in a statement . “This work includes updates to our booking, ticketing and distribution policies.”

The airline’s move follows a warning from banks, including Bank of America, which last week urged customers not to share their passwords with their AI assistants.

en.title: Apple Notes adds a powerful new advantage in iOS 27.3
en.summary: There’s no shortage of note-taking apps on the App Store, but Apple Notes has long been my favorite, and in iOS 27.3 it’s gaining a new advantage: extensive app controls via Siri AI. more…
en.body:
There’s no shortage of note-taking apps on the App Store, but Apple Notes has long been my favorite, and in iOS 27.3 it’s gaining a new advantage: extensive app controls via Siri AI.

Voice-driven computing is on the rise, with AI assistants—including Siri AI—now more capable and intelligent than ever.

Siri AI is already a big upgrade over the old Siri, but it’s getting even better in iOS 27.3.

As we reported last week , iOS 27.3 gives Siri AI many new capabilities across built-in Apple apps on your iPhone, iPad, Mac, and more.

The one I’ve been testing the most is Apple Notes. Siri has offered basic Notes-related functionality for years, but it gains a whole new set of powers with the new update.

Here’s everything Siri told me it can do in Notes as of iOS 27.3:

That’s a lot of capabilities that can all now be handled by Siri.

I have nearly 3,000 notes saved in Apple Notes and use the app every day, so it’s been fun seeing what Siri can now do for me. One common example is that I’ve been able to have Siri save a link to the webpage I’m currently viewing inside a note, and even specify exactly where in the note I want it to go.

In theory, third-party notes apps may be able to offer similar controls sometime next year when app skills officially launch . For now though, anyone who wants to control their notes app by voice—or via Spotlight, as I tend to do on my iPad Pro—have another reason to use Apple Notes.

Have you tried Siri AI’s new Notes features in iOS 27.3? Let us know in the comments.

en.title: Google pushes privacy angle as Gemini-powered smartglasses debut starting at $395
en.summary: The first Gemini smartglasses are a collab between Google, Samsung, Gentle Monster, and Warby Parker.
en.body:
Smartglasses have always faced an uphill road to acceptance. Not only is propping a computer up on your nose an uncomfortable proposition, but the privacy aspect has been vexing people since the Google Glass days . Now, Google is ready to take another swing at " intelligent eyewear " for the Gemini era after previewing its plans a couple of times. The first glasses are up for preorder today from Gentle Monster and Warby Parker, but they're no impulse buy.

These devices are a collaboration between Google, Samsung, and the aforementioned eyewear designers. Gentle Monster and Warby Parker have each designed a few different frames, with options for transparent and tinted lenses. Samsung is providing the computing hardware that fits inside them, and Google has the software covered.

Warby Parker has designed three frames for Google eyewear, called Alden, Reid, and Wren (see above). They are available with both standard optical and sun lenses in Pine, Saddle, and Jet Black colors at $395 and higher. Warby Parker is only selling devices in the US. Gentle Monster has gone a bit further with six styles, but Google hasn't told us any names for those yet. They come in dark red, pink, gray, and yellow colors and are available with clear, tinted, blue, or brown lenses. The Gentle Monster styles start a little higher at $449, and they will be available in the US and South Korea.

en.title: Google’s new Android XR glasses work with iOS, Made for iPhone certified
en.summary: Google today announced Android XR audio glasses called Intelligent Eyewear that notably support iOS with Made for iPhone certification. more…
en.body:
Google today announced Android XR audio glasses called Intelligent Eyewear that notably support iOS with Made for iPhone certification.

Hands-on: Google and Samsung’s vision for Android XR glasses is 20/20

Intelligent Eyewear is made by Samsung with frame designs from Gentle Monster and Warby Parker . There are 30 unique designs in total, and the frames weigh 40-44 grams with a 12-megapixel ultra-wide camera.

Google’s Glasses companion client for iOS handles compute, including HDR processing, and saves images and videos (up to 90 seconds) to Apple Photos. The Made for iPhone certification comes into play for Wi-Fi Aware connectivity that allows for fast media transfers.

On the privacy front, there is a blinking white indicator light when you use the camera to take pictures or record clips that are saved to your library. If the light is covered or disabled, the glasses will stop recording, with Android XR running a hardware check when charging.

Warby Parker

Gemini commands that use the camera, like visual search or translation, don’t trigger the light because those photos or videos are not saved anywhere, including Gemini History. Before that media reaches the cloud, Google redacts faces from video feeds and filters out bystander voices. This processing is done by the companion app. Additionally, that media isn’t used to train AI models or target ads.

Other key specifications include four microphones and two open-ear speakers. Besides voice commands with the “Hey Gemini” hotword, there is a touchpad that accepts taps and swipes. A physical on/off switch lets you wear Intelligent Eyewear as regular glasses.

On iOS, Gemini can make calls, send 1:1 messages (including via iMessage), and receive notifications.

Gentle Monster

Battery life is rated at nine hours on a single charge, while there’s a charging case that stores seven charges. Features include turn-by-turn Google Maps directions and real-time translation. On the streaming front, there’s support for Apple Music, Spotify, YouTube Music, and Audible.

Google’s Android XR glasses require an iPhone 13 Pro or newer.

Warby Parker Intelligent Eyewear is available in three frame designs, starting at $395 for optical and sun styles. Gentle Monster Intelligent Eyewear is available in the US and South Korea from $449.

Pre-orders open today with retail availability on December 10.

en.title: Apple HomeView review: A versatile smart display and Siri-powered home hub
en.summary: With its first smart display, Apple provides a lot of convenience for a variety of tasks in your home.
en.body:
The company’s smart screen debut heavily relies on an iPhone or iPad — for better and for worse.

Apple's entry into the smart display category was rumored for years. By the time its debut home hub device arrives this week, the company will be nearly a decade behind its main rivals in the space. In true Apple fashion, it refused to rush new products just because most of the competition was doing it. Now that the HomeView ($299) is here, Apple is hoping the iPhone faithful will like its mix of elevated design and newly expanded Siri capabilities .

Unlike smart displays from Amazon and Google, Apple's approach relies on a companion device. That means you'll need either an iPhone or an iPad to mirror apps using technology similar to CarPlay. As you'd imagine, that means the HomeView's usefulness, like CarPlay's, is directly tied to how much you use Apple's core apps — things like Messages, Calendar, Photos, Reminders and others. You'll also need to have some smart home devices to make the most of the smart display and be willing to use Safari as your recipe box. If all of that is OK to you, and if you're willing to give Siri access to personal data inside some of those apps, the HomeView can quickly become a very versatile device with something for your whole family.

I have fond memories of the iMac G4 . It was the first computer I used in a design lab in college, and I loved how I could reposition the display to suit the task at hand. The first time I saw the HomeView, those memories flooded back. Apple's smart home display doesn't exactly replicate the G4 styling, but it's close enough for a decent nostalgia hit for me.

The HomeView essentially consists of two parts: a cylindrical, domed base and a 7-inch Liquid Retina display. At least, that's if you get the tabletop version. The wall-mounted option is just the screen, and you'll have to pay at least $59.95 for a mount. Every version of the HomeView has two full-range drivers in the display itself. The base houses additional components, like a down-firing woofer and a pair of force-canceling passive radiators for fuller sound with more bass than the wall-mounted models.

That display has an LED-backlit multi-touch IPS panel that offers a 1,088 x 1,088 resolution at 200 pixels per inch. Apple says it also added an oleophobic fingerprint-resistant coating to cut down on grime from everyday use. There's an ambient light sensor that enables the HomeView to adjust both brightness and warmth as needed. If it's in direct sunlight, you can expect the maximum 500 nits, but at night, it can dial things down to just 0.3 nits — the lowest brightness ever on an Apple display. The company believes this makes it perfect for a nightstand, if you're willing to have a camera pointed at or near your bed.

The HomeView's display has bezels like an iPad and the shape of a large Apple Watch. Unlike either of those devices, though, it has no physical buttons for controls. All of the interaction is done via swipes and taps on the touchscreen itself, or, as I'll elaborate on in a bit, with your voice. And unlike that iMac I'm nostalgic for, you can only tilt the display — you can't adjust its height. While that will suit most of your needs, I'm sure there are a lot of people who would've liked the ability to change the height or rotate the screen as well. Once you do adjust the way it tilts, a built-in accelerometer detects the new angle and alters the audio performance of the display's two drivers to match it.

Another item to discuss in terms of design is the HomeView's lone port. Around back, there's a single USB-C jack for power. Apple ships the standard version of the device with a USB-C to USB-C cable and a 30-watt power adapter. If you opt for the USB-C wall mount, which already costs $59.99, you'll need to purchase the power adapter separately. The company offers a 40W dynamic power adapter (up to 60W max) for $39 while the minimum required power supply ( 20W ) will cost you $19. Obviously, the AC wired and PoE (power over Ethernet) wired mounts won't need a power adapter.

And lastly, there's the matter of color. For the standard (table or countertop) version of HomeView, you can choose from Silver, Starlight, Rose Pink or Space Gray options. On those, the sides and back of the display match the base. For the wall-mounted version, you can only pick between Silver and Space Gray. And, just in case you need the reminder, both HomeView models are the same price ($299).

One of the HomeView's most helpful traits is its ability to put Siri AI front and center in your home. The smart device runs on Apple's A18 chip, the processor that debuted with the iPhone 16 line in 2024. The company is using it here for its Secure Exclaves which give it the ability to process camera and microphone feeds on-device in a manner that can't be accessed by Apple. The company explained that this enables the HomeView to recognize your face and voice, or that of other users in your home, without exposing any of the data to the operating system.

That's important, because Siri AI now has access to more of your personal data, like your conversations in Messages, info from your Calendar invites and other bits of "personal context" from various apps. Of course, you have to opt-in to all of this by enabling Apple Intelligence on your iPhone or iPad, and you can limit which apps Siri can index data from. If you do decide to use the system, I can attest that it works well on the HomeView, though it's merely another vessel for the larger AI system.

During a lengthy conversation about lighthouses in North Carolina, Siri gave me information about visiting a variety of locations in the state. It provided information that I didn't specifically ask for, like which ones were still active, and got more comprehensive when my follow-up query was a bit vague. For example, when I asked "Which lighthouse is the easiest to get to?" Siri responded with both a list of ones you can park close to and highlighted the one that requires the least amount of climbing.

Siri was able to check my calendar to see if I was free to take the trip on a certain date and provided travel time from my house (including follow-up questions about the cities I'd pass through). I was finally able to stump the AI when I asked about "good hotels" near the Currituck Beach Lighthouse in Corolla, but even still, things felt more natural and conversational than interactions I've had with Siri in the past.

At times, Siri showed text answers on the HomeView in addition to reciting the info. When I asked about driving time or my schedule, a preview of the best route and the specific day on my calendar popped up respectively. What's more, I got a notification on my phone from the Home app letting me know Siri responded to a request for personal content. But it's important to remember that HomeView is just a conduit for Siri AI and its newly expanded abilities. These same things can be done on an iPhone or other compatible Apple devices, meaning you don't really have to spend $300 on a dedicated display for these tools.

One final note on security: Since the HomeView is heavily reliant on an iPhone or iPad, those devices must be nearby and recently unlocked (and enrolled in the shared home) for Siri to access personal data. The HomeView uses facial and voice recognition to know who's speaking, and to know when they walk away, so prying eyes can't see your texts if they rush over after you've been looking at Messages or other potentially sensitive apps. Guests or family members who don't have an iPhone or iPad can still use basic functions (control smart home devices, check weather, play music, etc), including asking Siri rudimentary questions.

When I first spent time with the HomeView last month, the feature I was most excited about was the recipe integration in Safari. I'm happy to report that feeling remains, for the most part, but there's one caveat that does impact the overall experience.

Let's back up for a second. On the HomeView, you can view a recipe link in Safari from your iPhone by holding it close to the display (just like you do to pass audio from your phone to a HomePod). Once the page loads, you'll see a cooking icon (a spoon and recipe card) in the bottom right corner. Tapping that will launch the HomeView's streamlined mode for the kitchen, which shows a recipe image with the dish's name, creator, cooking time and servings. There are two options underneath: Ingredients and Start Cooking.

The Ingredients option gives you a checklist-style collection of what you'll need for the recipe. If you need to add things to a shopping list in Reminders, Siri can do that for you. I had no trouble getting the AI assistant to add various ingredients to different shopping lists I have in that app (Costco, grocery store, etc). The HomeView will show its work by displaying the new entry in the Reminders app, and a Live Activities shortcut at the top allows you to quickly get back to the recipe with a tap.

Once you hit Start Cooking, the recipe's steps are divided into swipeable slides with inline shortcuts for any timers you need. Or, at least that's how it's supposed to be. While testing the HomeView, I pulled in recipes from my go-to cooks, and while some of them worked just like Apple advertised, others did not. This isn't a massive deal breaker, as you can still read the recipe's steps, but once you've experienced the correctly formatted version, it's hard to go back.

Going back means you'll get all of the steps on a single slide, requiring you to scroll instead of swipe. This is a long block of text, which can be overwhelming, especially compared to the short, easy-to-follow slides that alleviate some of the stress from following complicated instructions. And if you ever need to peek back at that ingredients list, the properly formatted versions have an always-present shortcut in the bottom right corner. To be clear, the formatting isn't an Apple problem; it's entirely up to the creator or publisher to present their recipes a certain way. I'm just pointing this all out to say Apple is advertising the ideal scenario, which is honestly an excellent experience, but you may not encounter it every time you cook with HomeView.

Another big piece of the HomeView puzzle is its ability to act as a smart home hub. With the Home app and devices compatible with HomeKit and Matter, this display becomes the command center for your cameras, thermostat, lighting and more. There's a Home dashboard that shows everything you've connected to the system. You can then create scenes and automations, or ask Siri to handle those for you.

We'll get to HomeView customization in a bit, but it's important to mention two Home faces here. The Home Modular face puts your favorite smart home devices on the same screen thanks to customizable widgets. These give you control over each connected gadget, including the ability to check a camera feed, without opening any apps on your phone. Of course, you can always ask Siri to do things for you by summoning the assistant on the HomeView. I'm sure Apple's AI is tired of adjusting my thermostat at this point, as that's what I've primarily been doing during my testing.

There's also a Home Camera face that's all video, all the time. Here, you can livestream up to nine feeds at once, giving you the ability to keep tabs on things wherever you have cameras positioned. If a visitor is detected, you can just tap on the HomeView to unlock a smart door lock (provided you have one of those, of course). We are a Blink household, though, and those aren't yet compatible with HomeKit, so I wasn't able to test any of Apple's camera features.

If you have an iCloud+ subscription, HomeView works with compatible security cameras (again, HomeKit and Matter) to detect people, pets, packages and vehicles. When any of those are seen, you'll get a notification and a live feed on the display. HomeView can also detect smoke or carbon monoxide alarms and send alerts to your iPhone, iPad or Apple Watch — even when you're away from home. That feature, known as Sound Recognition, is also available on the HomePod and HomePod mini.

The HomeView's speakers make it a solid option for music, podcasts and other audio entertainment. But, despite its crisp, vivid display, the device is not well-suited for watching videos. That's OK though, because right now, the only video app that's available on HomeView is Apple TV. And unless you like watching your shows within a thin band that sits in the middle of a square display, flanked by thick black bars on the top and bottom, you, too, will find the video experience on HomeView underwhelming. I would love to see Apple bring F1 multiview to this display though, putting two small alternate feeds below the main broadcast. Yes, they'd be tiny, but at least that's a better use of the space and eliminates the awkward black bars.

The HomeView runs on the same platform as CarPlay , which is why the various video streaming apps you have on your iPhone don't show up on this device. Apple says third-party developers are welcome to enable their apps for use on the HomeView, but doing so would also mean optimizing them for CarPlay. Only time will tell if developers are going to go through the extra steps of making that happen.

When it comes to audio-only content though, the HomeView is great. I'd classify the sound quality here as the midpoint between the HomePod mini and the larger HomePod. I've been reviewing the tabletop HomeView with a base, so I've enjoyed the added woofer and passive radiators, which balance out full-range drivers with extra bass. Across a variety of genres, bass is tight and punchy, and vocals cut through the mix clearly. The system never loses other instruments either, as you can easily pick up the guitars in Anberlin's "Gravity." Switch to something more chill, like Sam Barber's "If I May," and the acoustic instruments lay a base for the singer's unique vocals. Drums are more subdued here, and the HomeView does well to keep them from overpowering the mix.

I should also note the HomeView can get pretty darn loud. I measured 87dB with my Apple Watch standing right in front of the device. But I should also warn you that it's not a comfortable listening volume if you're standing close to the display. It might be nice for a party, but you'll likely stay around 50 percent or less for the most part.

Spatial Audio with Dolby Atmos is available on the HomeView for compatible music, movies and shows. However, given the compact stature of the device and its limited sonic prowess, you're more likely to notice the excellent overall clarity and even-handed tuning more than any dimensional effects. While watching an episode of Masters of the Air, for example, I found the sound perfectly fine, but wouldn't classify it as very immersive.

Apple included a few more entertainment-related conveniences on the HomeView that add utility. For one, it works with the HomePod, HomePod mini and AirPlay-compatible speakers for multiroom audio, which allows you to play the same thing everywhere or pick specific songs for each room. When listening to songs from Apple Music, you'll see animated album artwork if an artist has it, and lyrics are available with a single tap. And just like you can with your iPhone and HomePod speakers, you can handoff content from your phone to the HomeView just by placing your handset in front of the display.

The HomeView may look like an enlarged Apple Watch's screen, but the two devices also overlap in another area: faces. These screens are what you see when the HomeView is in what I like to call rest mode, when it's just sitting there not being actively used. You can have it just be a clock, as there are three faces just for that purpose, or display your calendar or the weather. There's also an animated Snoopy face that updates based on the time of day, weather, holidays and sporting events. Then there are the two Home faces that work with smart home devices that I already mentioned.

Those all have their purpose, but my two favorites are the Photos and Modular faces. The former makes the HomeView a digital picture frame and you can get specific about what shows up there. You can opt for it to cycle through photos of specific events (Memories), people, pets or cities, for example, but you can also set up Shared Albums that it will source from. If you do that last one, new photos will automatically appear every time they're added to the collection. The Modular face is what I've used most, as its customizable collection of widgets puts the calendar, date, time and weather in one spot. Of course, you can pick and choose what shows up here based on your needs or preferences, you're not forced to use the same combination I do.

The best thing about faces is that you can easily switch between them by swiping horizontally on one. A long press brings up the face customization interface where you're free to fine-tune things like color and widgets (where available) to your heart's content.

One feature that Apple has spent a lot of time showing off on the HomeView is FaceTime. The smart display has a 12-megapixel Center Stage camera in its top bezel, which means you can conduct video chats without reaching for your iPhone. Of course, the Center Stage software will keep you centered in the frame as you move around, which will be handy if you need to take a call from the kitchen while you're cooking, for example. You can start FaceTime calls on the HomeView, or you can hand them off from your iPhone. I'll also note that you can take voice calls from the HomeView, and in general, the device works well for both types of chats.

Find My is also available on the HomeView, allowing you to locate everything from your iPhone to your AirPods, or anything that has an AirTag attached to it. Of course, you can also use this to find family and friends who are sharing their location with you. The intercom feature from HomePods is on the HomeView as well, which comes in handy if you have multiple Apple speakers spread throughout your house. It also works with the iPhone, iPad and Apple Watch, plus you can send and receive intercom messages from anywhere — not just inside your home.

Lastly, Live Activities displays real-time info for a variety of tasks on HomeView. Like it does on your iPhone, the feature puts your progress at the top of the display on a floating, tappable button. Live Activities on the HomeView are a bit limited though, only capable of showing active timers/alarms, FaceTime calls, Safari media playback and Now Playing controls for Apple Music or Apple TV. I found it also surfaced audio controls for my go-to podcast app Pocket Casts as well. One thing that doesn't show up there that I wish it did is Live Activities from the Sports app. It would be great if the live scores for my favorite teams or an update on who's leading the F1 grand prix were available at a glance.

Apple is years behind the competition when it comes to smart displays. The company's two main rivals in this category, Amazon and Google, have been honing their products since 2017 and 2018 respectively. The premise has always been similar to Apple's: a combination display and speaker that's a conduit for each company's virtual assistant — or in 2026 terms, each company's AI.

Amazon's current Echo Show lineup has six options, ranging from 5 inches up to 21 inches, with the largest models ditching the speaker base for a wall mount or stand. The most affordable, the Echo Show 5 , is $100. Google's current slate of smart displays is much more modest, with only the aging second-generation Nest Hub and Nest Hub Max as the available options. Those are going for $100 and $229 respectively, and only the pricier of the two has a built-in camera for video calls.

Apple may have lagged behind the competition on introducing a smart display, but the HomeView checks a lot of boxes that make it a very powerful option for iPhone users. It's also more elegantly designed than all of its main competitors. The ability to automatically distinguish between different family members, and for Siri to pull in personalized context for each person, makes this a useful home hub. When you factor in the cooking assistance, smart home compatibility and FaceTime chops, the HomeView can easily become the command center for any household. Just be sure to keep your iPhone (or iPad) handy if you want to make the most of it.

en.title: The first batch of Android XR smartglasses made me rethink my stance on specs without displays
en.summary: Google's first run of intelligent eyewear has a lot to offer.
en.body:
I still want models with built-in screens, but Google’s first run of intelligent eyewear has a lot to offer.

The first device powered by Android XR came out last year when Samsung released the Galaxy XR headset . But this fall, Google is taking its augmented reality platform in a different direction with the launch of intelligent eyewear from partners such as Warby Parker and Gentle Monster . This gives Google its own version of lightweight smartglasses to rival competitors like the third-gen Ray-Ban Meta line , and after testing them out, it made me reconsider my feelings about smart specs without built-in displays.

As this first generation of intelligent eyewear is a bit of a departure from previous Android XR devices, I think it's important to get some of the basics out of the way first. For this family of specs, Google is in charge of the OS while Samsung is handling much of the tech — including things like the cameras, mics, touch sensors and more. All of that then gets handed over to Warby Parker and Gentle Monster, who are in charge of the glasses design, lenses, general sales and customer support.

Right off the bat, this seems like a great division of responsibilities because it allows each company to do what they're best at. Google handles the software, Samsung takes care of the hardware and the real glasses makers ensure you have good-looking frames with the right prescriptions (you can even opt for transition/photochromic lenses). And right out of the gate, it feels like there's already a lot of interesting styles and color combos to choose from, regardless if you're a bit more fashion-forward or if you, like me, prefer a more traditional frame.

Another important thing to note is that while Gentle Monster's eyewear will be a touch more expensive than Warby Parker's models ($449 and $395, respectively), they will have the same general tech specs. Those include the same 2GB of RAM and 64GB of storage, a 12MP camera (that also handles up to 3K video), stereo speakers, far-field mics and a built-in touch sensor. Battery life is also the same across the board with around nine hours of use on a single charge, while the case for the glasses stores enough juice for multiple full charges.

Furthermore, you won't be required to have a paid Gemini plan to use any of the features of the glasses; it's all free. These glasses will even work with both Android devices and iPhones with feature parity across both OSes. That said, there won't be any options with a built-in display, which means Google won't have a true rival to the Meta Ray-Ban Display glasses, at least not yet.

When it comes to features, it's no surprise that these glasses have a lot of overlap with the Ray-Ban Meta specs. There's a physical button near the right temple for capturing images: A short press takes a picture while a long press records videos. There's also a touch sensor built into the right arm for doing stuff like controlling volume, pausing audio or dismissing Gemini. And of course, the glasses are connected to your phone wirelessly (either Bluetooth or Wi-Fi depending on the situation) so you have access to streaming music, notifications, messages, supported apps and more. However, the real lynchpin of the entire platform is Google's AI, which can be easily summoned via voice controls or by performing a long press on the touch panel.

Now I'll admit that I don't interact with Gemini all that often when I'm using a phone or a laptop. When I already have access to a screen, a keyboard and all sorts of dedicated apps, so I find I can often perform tasks faster manually than asking an AI assistant to do them. But when wearing smartglasses, it's a whole different story. If you want to respond to a text, get turn-by-turn directions or start some tunes, you can do all that hands-free with simple voice commands while keeping your phone in your pocket. Granted, that is sort of table stakes for smartglasses these days, but being able to walk around with your head up while dodging traffic or other pedestrians can't be understated.

But it goes deeper, because thanks to Gemini's intelligence and persistent memory between conversations, the AI in your glasses has a much deeper understanding of how to help you. Instead of constantly having to say a wake word all the time, you can have more natural back and forth dialogue. This allows you to get updates on your events, make adjustments to questions and pick up on previous queries even when they happen throughout the course of your day (you can specify how long you want Gemini to remember conversations).

Where things get really interesting is the combination of computer vision and AI, which allowed me to do things like pick up a physical invite card and simply ask Gemini to add it to my calendar. No need to grab my phone, open up an app and add details like the time, date and location myself. I was also able to do things like simply look at a bunch of different ingredients and ask Gemini to make a smoothie from what was in front of me. It can even do rough estimates for how much of a certain food has been added, so if you're not worried about being super precise, you can leave your measuring cups in a drawer. And if you run out of certain foods, you can easily tell Gemini to add something to your grocery list.

Then there are other features like live translation, which feels kind of magical. The glasses are designed so that the mics are directed in a cone-shaped space in front of you, so that even in a room with other conversations going on, the glasses don't get confused. Not only does this let you switch speakers naturally just by looking at someone else, Gemini will even adjust the output of a translation to sound similar to the original speaker. This allows you to follow along in real-time almost as well as someone who speaks the language naturally.

That said, the thing that impressed me the most about these Android XR glasses is the platform itself. Compared to some rivals where a lot of features feel like a work in progress, Google's OS feels much more mature. This includes little touches like dedicated sounds when Gemini accesses your camera, when the glasses take a photo or video, when Gemini leverages external AI and more. Google has done a pretty good job of translating a lot of the most important features you use on your phone to a medium without a screen.

Then there's Google's approach to privacy, which looks to be a step up from the competition. In addition to each pair of glasses coming with an LED indicator that blocks you from taking pictures or videos when it's covered up or disabled, Google also isn't supporting features like livestreaming video directly from the specs. Furthermore, Google says images and info sent to Gemini will stay on your device and will not be used to train AI or for ad targeting. That might not sound like much, but considering Google owns YouTube and generates billions from advertising, the simple act of leaving money on the table in favor of privacy is a welcome departure from Meta's glasses. Those have always felt like they are meant to expand the reach of Facebook and Instagram.

The one caveat to all this is that you do have to buy into talking to and relying rather heavily on Gemini. I'm still not sure I'm 100 percent on board with that, but at least for me, these glasses make a better argument for always-on AI support than almost any other class of device I've used. So while I'm still waiting for companies to deliver streamlined specs with built-in displays, these audio-first options feel like much more than a stepping stone towards that. They're surprisingly full-featured, and I don't think it's a stretch to say that compared to rival assistants like Siri, Muse and others, Gemini is the smartest of the bunch. So even if you primarily want these for playing music, keeping tabs on your schedule and getting occasional help from AI, Google's first batch of Android XR-powered intelligent eyewear feels like it's already jumped to the front of the pack.

Pre-orders for the new family of Android XR intelligent eyewear from both Warby Parker and Gentle Monster begin today with official sales slated for December 10.

en.title: Google really needs you to know it cares about smart glasses privacy
en.summary: Yes, it's a bit attention-seeking, but some of these policies are genuinely good.
en.body:
Public trust in smart glasses is very important for selling lots of smart glasses.

The world has changed in the ten years since Snap first launched its camera-equipped Spectacles . Not only has the smart glasses market grown, the number of people sharing videos online has also jumped significantly. Nowadays, thanks to the rise of platforms like TikTok and Reels, anyone can be an influencer. And the possibility of innocent passersby inadvertently being included in a viral clip is far higher than it was.

It is in this climate that Google launches its intelligent eyewear devices today. This year has already seen Meta catch heat for what people called its "pervert glasses" or "creep glasses." In addition to making people feel uncomfortable about being spied on or filmed without their consent, the controversy has also discouraged existing users of those glasses from continuing to wear them, not to mention possibly putting off potential buyers.

Google has been working on this launch for years , and it can be easy to see why it doesn't want its own camera-equipped glasses to suffer the same backlash or be painted by the same brush. Perhaps that's why it's taking pains to make its privacy policies around the intelligent eyewear platform clear today. It's published a blog post outlining the privacy protections it's bringing to the platform, and they don't just revolve around preventing tampering with the LED indicator lights. Google is taking a fairly comprehensive approach that goes beyond device-specific measures, and includes using its wide sphere of influence to prevent surreptitious videos spreading online. In fact, Juston Payne, the lead for XR at Google, told Engadget that there are quite a few ways privacy protection has been considered.

Let's start with what's happening on the glasses. It's basically table stakes at this point, but they all have an LED light on them to indicate when someone is taking a picture or recording a video. The light, which sits on the left side of the frame while the camera is next to the right eye, has sensors to detect if it's covered or tampered with and will prevent the capture of pictures or video.

"Unfortunately, some of the glasses that have launched in the past launched without any kind of detection for those things, and that broke trust." Payne said. "And that's a problem," he added. He also said Google's methods are "pretty effective," though that's something that we'll have to test for ourselves to verify.

And just as there are bad actors who will continue to try to break security protections for any safe in the world or online, there will be people attempting to get around Google's anti-tampering measures here. Payne said "there will always be ways around what we build, and then we'll try to fix those holes," and that he expects there will be an ongoing back-and-forth. "But nonetheless, we're very happy with where we're starting on this one."

One of the main functions of Google's smart glasses is the ability for Gemini AI to use the camera to see what the wearer is looking at and provide more relevant information. During this process, the company says that the camera visuals won't be stored in your Gemini history. When there are faces in view, Google says "your glasses are also designed to automatically redact bystanders' faces before Gemini processes the visuals."

The camera stream also won't be used in AI training or ad targeting, and Google says any data that is sent off the glasses for processing, say in the cloud or on your phone, is encrypted for transit. It's also promising to bring the Private AI Compute processing platform to glasses, enabling these new devices to use the "hardware-secured sealed cloud environment" for greater processing.

While the camera may be the most obvious recording sensor on these devices, they also have four microphones onboard to allow you to speak to Gemini or get translations for people around you. Google uses beamforming to help focus on the individuals you're looking at when deciding whose speech to translate, and the company also said it "designed Gemini to focus on your voice by default, and not other voices around you, using directional microphones on the glasses."

Payne said that the microphones will filter out "all the world audio, as we call it, the bystander audio," It helps prevent accidental recording of people in your vicinity, but also improves Gemini's effectiveness by making sure it doesn't confuse someone else's heated argument as your query.

Of course, to make the glasses more useful, you'll have to grant it access to your apps and personal information. The intelligent eyewear can work with apps like Messages, Keep or YouTube Music, for instance, to send replies or create lists for you. Like on most phones, you'll have to grant permission to specific apps before they can access the camera on your glasses, and even after you do, you can still add or revoke access for every app.

Google also said you can view your past interactions with Gemini, delete individual chats or all of them. You'll also be able to decide if your conversations are used to train AI. And to make sure there's no confusion over whether you left the glasses on or off, and if the microphones or camera might still be tuning in, all the new eyewear have a power switch with a clear red indicator to tell you when they've been shut down.

Most intriguing are the measures Google is implementing across its entire ecosystem. The company said it has protections in place "across Google apps and services to deter misuse of the glasses," and they're pretty far-reaching.

For one thing, Google Shopping and Google Ads will "ban the sale and advertising of stickers or accessories designed to hide recording lights."

The company is also working to cull the demand for videos of a harassing or creepy nature. Payne said that one of the problems Google has seen is a small number of people "who use glasses to take creepy videos."

YouTube will "prohibit content that depicts things like harassment and unwanted sexualization. Any video uploaded to YouTube — whether it's recorded on a phone, a camera, or glasses — has to follow these policies, and videos that don't are removed."

There are also considerations for apps that request permission to use the cameras on these devices. "There's multiple approval layers if an app wants to use the camera," Payne said. "And there's actually some use cases that we're just blanket cutting off."

To that end, Google said that the Play Store and API policies will "prohibit apps from using the camera for social live-streaming or real-time facial identification, and from changing the behavior of the outer indicator light." This live-streaming restriction also applies to YouTube.

Of course, since the eyewear will be compatible with iOS devices as well, it's possible that someone finds an app of that nature in the App Store and uses it. And though Google may ban the advertisement or sale of physical goods that can be used to hide the LED indicator, people could very easily procure one on Amazon or Temu. There's more that needs to be done against this problem, and Google alone cannot cover all bases.

Sure, there's the honor system approach that most modern recording devices already use. Things like requiring an 18+ Google account to activate an intelligent eyewear device and asking users to agree to not recording others without permission or in sensitive places are in place here as well.

But the responsibility of prevention of misuse doesn't just fall to the user or Google. There needs to be greater collaboration across the industry for these measures to be effective. Payne said that Google is sharing these statements now in an attempt to set an example and send a message. "We hope that it resonates with people, and we hope that as a byproduct of that, some others in this space say, 'You know what? We should probably tighten up some of our policies.'"

Payne believes that there is time to regain the public's trust. He said that while there is momentum building in the smart glasses space, it is still early days for the category. It allows the company a chance to "reset this conversation a bit, raise the bar on privacy."

If it's able to get the attention and cooperation of other players in the space, Google stands to benefit. "We think that that will then earn a lot of trust back in the category, then we can focus a lot on how cool and valuable these are."

es.title: Una retina artificial convierte la luz infrarroja en señales eléctricas para estimular las neuronas del ojo
es.summary: Una investigación publicada en Nature Electronics presenta un implante retiniano capaz de transformar la luz infrarroja cercana en impulsos eléctricos. El dispositivo ha conseguido generar respuestas neuronales en ratones con degeneración de la retina y abre nuevas posibilidades para el desarrollo de prótesis visuales. La ingeniería biomédica continúa explorando nuevas formas de recuperar parcialmente la […] La entrada Una retina artificial convierte la luz infrarroja en señales eléctricas para estimular las neuronas del ojo se publicó primero en Conticgo .
es.body:
Una investigación publicada en Nature Electronics presenta un implante retiniano capaz de transformar la luz infrarroja cercana en impulsos eléctricos. El dispositivo ha conseguido generar respuestas neuronales en ratones con degeneración de la retina y abre nuevas posibilidades para el desarrollo de prótesis visuales.

La ingeniería biomédica continúa explorando nuevas formas de recuperar parcialmente la percepción visual en personas con enfermedades degenerativas de la retina. Una de las últimas investigaciones en este campo propone una solución basada en una retina artificial capaz de transformar la luz infrarroja cercana en señales eléctricas que estimulan directamente las neuronas del ojo.

El trabajo, publicado en abril de 2026 en la revista científica Nature Electronics , ha sido desarrollado por investigadores de distintas instituciones de Corea del Sur. Su propuesta combina sensores fotosensibles, microelectrodos de metal líquido y un sistema electrónico implantable que permite activar determinadas células de la retina.

Los experimentos realizados en ratones, incluidos animales con degeneración retiniana, han demostrado que el dispositivo puede provocar respuestas neuronales ante estímulos de luz infrarroja.

La visión natural comienza cuando los fotorreceptores de la retina, conocidos como conos y bastones, detectan la luz y la transforman en señales eléctricas. Estas señales se procesan en diferentes capas retinianas y posteriormente se transmiten al cerebro a través del nervio óptico.

Sin embargo, enfermedades como la retinosis pigmentaria provocan la degeneración progresiva de los fotorreceptores. Aunque estas células pueden llegar a desaparecer, otras estructuras de la retina, como las células ganglionares, pueden conservar parte de su funcionalidad.

La nueva tecnología pretende aprovechar precisamente esta capacidad.

El implante incorpora una matriz de fototransistores sensibles a la luz infrarroja cercana. Estos pequeños componentes detectan la radiación y generan una respuesta eléctrica que se transmite a través de unos microelectrodos situados en contacto con las neuronas retinianas.

De esta manera, el dispositivo evita depender de los fotorreceptores dañados y utiliza una vía alternativa para transmitir información visual al cerebro.

Uno de los aspectos más innovadores de esta investigación es el material empleado para fabricar los electrodos.

Los investigadores han desarrollado unos pequeños pilares tridimensionales de metal líquido, elaborados a partir de una aleación de galio e indio. Su estructura flexible permite adaptarse mejor a la superficie irregular de la retina y establecer un contacto más cercano con las células ganglionares.

Esta característica es importante porque los electrodos rígidos convencionales pueden generar problemas cuando se implantan en tejidos biológicos tan delicados.

Además, los extremos de estos microelectrodos incorporan nanopartículas de platino que mejoran la transmisión de carga eléctrica y facilitan la estimulación neuronal.

El dispositivo también incluye un filtro óptico ultrafino, de aproximadamente 360 nanómetros de grosor, diseñado para permitir el paso de determinadas longitudes de onda infrarrojas y controlar la entrada de luz visible en los sensores.

Para comprobar el funcionamiento de esta retina artificial, el equipo realizó diferentes experimentos tanto en tejidos retinianos aislados como en animales vivos.

Las pruebas incluyeron ratones sanos y ratones con degeneración retiniana, utilizados como modelo experimental de ceguera asociada a la pérdida de fotorreceptores.

Los investigadores observaron que, cuando el dispositivo recibía luz infrarroja cercana, los fototransistores generaban impulsos eléctricos capaces de activar las células ganglionares.

Además, mediante registros de actividad cerebral y pruebas de comportamiento, comprobaron que los estímulos llegaban hasta la corteza visual de los animales.

Uno de los resultados más relevantes fue que los ratones con degeneración retiniana también mostraron respuestas ante la estimulación infrarroja. Esto indica que el sistema puede aprovechar determinadas neuronas que permanecen funcionales incluso cuando los fotorreceptores han sufrido un deterioro importante.

Los estudios de biocompatibilidad también mostraron resultados iniciales favorables. En los animales evaluados durante seis meses no se observaron signos relevantes de inflamación o deterioro del tejido asociados al implante.

La investigación podría abrir una nueva vía para desarrollar prótesis visuales destinadas a personas que han perdido los fotorreceptores como consecuencia de enfermedades degenerativas de la retina.

En patologías como la retinosis pigmentaria, la pérdida progresiva de conos y bastones puede provocar una reducción importante de la visión e incluso llegar a causar ceguera.

Sin embargo, las células ganglionares y otras neuronas internas pueden permanecer relativamente conservadas durante determinadas fases de la enfermedad.

La propuesta de los investigadores consiste en aprovechar esas estructuras para transmitir información mediante estimulación eléctrica, sin depender de los fotorreceptores originales.

Otro aspecto interesante es que el dispositivo trabaja con luz infrarroja cercana, una región del espectro electromagnético que el ojo humano no puede percibir de forma natural. Esto permitiría crear un canal artificial de percepción que complemente la visión visible que todavía conserve la persona.

Los investigadores también plantean que esta tecnología podría adaptarse en el futuro para detectar otras longitudes de onda, aunque todavía es necesario estudiar sus posibilidades.

A pesar de los resultados obtenidos, esta retina artificial todavía se encuentra en una fase experimental.

Los ensayos se han realizado en ratones y no existen resultados que permitan afirmar que el dispositivo pueda utilizarse ya en personas con retinosis pigmentaria u otras enfermedades degenerativas.

Antes de plantear su aplicación clínica será necesario estudiar su seguridad a largo plazo, mejorar su miniaturización, reducir el consumo energético y comprobar su estabilidad después de periodos prolongados de implantación.

También será fundamental investigar cómo se traduce la estimulación eléctrica en una percepción visual útil para las personas. Activar las neuronas retinianas no significa recuperar automáticamente una visión natural.

No obstante, el trabajo publicado en Nature Electronics representa un avance relevante en el desarrollo de prótesis visuales y demuestra cómo la combinación de microelectrónica y materiales biocompatibles puede abrir nuevas posibilidades para intervenir sobre el sistema visual.

Si te ha gustado esta noticia no te pierdas las últimas novedades en tiflotectnología en nuestro apartado de noticias y redes sociales .

en.title: Clicklet
en.summary: Clicklet lets the Camera Control button on your iPhone start your Apple Shortcuts. Pick one shortcut to launch with a press, or turn on Menu mode and choose from a few favorites each time. Clicklet opens Apple Shortcuts to run your workflow, so you'll see the usual Shortcuts screens, along with any permission prompts or app handoffs your shortcut needs. en.title: Apple TV introduces new Sign Language interpretation feature
en.summary: Today, Apple announced a new accessibility feature on the Apple TV app offering sign language interpretation for supported titles.
en.body:
Text of this article

November 10, 2026

UPDATE

Apple TV introduces new Sign Language interpretation feature

New accessibility feature debuts Friday, November 13, with the streaming premiere of Being Heumann

Today, Apple announced a new accessibility feature for the Apple TV app that gives viewers the option to watch supported titles with accompanying sign language interpretation. 1 The feature will be available on Friday, November 13, alongside the global streaming premiere of Being Heumann , a film based on the true story of disability rights activist Judy Heumann, on Apple TV.

In addition to Being Heumann, interpretation for American Sign Language (ASL) and British Sign Language (BSL) will be available for the movie F1. Later this year, Way of the Warrior Kid and Greyhound will follow, with more Apple Original titles to come. When turned on in Apple TV app settings, the Sign Language option will appear on supported Apple Original titles.

“At Apple, we believe everyone should be able to enjoy great stories and entertainment,” said Sarah Herrlinger, Apple’s senior director of Global Accessibility Policy and Initiatives. “Bringing sign language interpretation to Apple TV is an exciting step forward in making the viewing experience more accessible and inclusive for Deaf audiences. Accessibility is a core value at Apple, and we’re proud to continue creating experiences that allow more people to enjoy the content they love.”

Designed with Native Signers in the Deaf Community

Apple TV offers a sign language experience that’s designed and tested by Deaf and native signers. Each performance is carefully crafted to fit and complement the Apple Original film it interprets.

“It’s incredibly meaningful to see our beautiful language authentically represented onscreen,” said Daniel Durant, who appears in Being Heumann and directed the film’s sign language interpretation. “Bringing this experience to life required a lot of care to ensure every translation captured the emotion and meaning of the story. I’m proud to have been part of Being Heumann and thrilled to see Apple TV supporting greater accessibility for Deaf audiences.”

New Ways to Discover Titles with Sign Language

Titles with sign language interpretation will be labeled with a Sign Language icon, making it easy to know when the option is available. Viewers can enable the feature in Apple TV app settings, then press the Sign Language button while watching. Search will also make it easier to find titles that feature sign language with simple phrases like “with ASL.”

As sign language interpretation becomes more widely available across streaming services, the new “Movies & Shows with American Sign Language” collection on the Apple TV app will offer viewers a simple way to explore titles featuring sign language, in one dedicated destination.

Being Heumann

In Being Heumann , Judy Heumann (Ruth Madeley) — scrappy, defiant, and done being treated like a burden — turns her outrage into a revolution. In San Francisco in 1977, she and more than 100 disability rights protesters organize a sit-in to send a very loud message: The system is broken — not us. The film marks the second collaboration between Apple Original Films and writer-director Siân Heder, who directed the multi-Academy Award-winning film CODA, which made history as the first film with a predominantly Deaf cast to receive the Best Picture honor.

Being Heumann premieres globally on Apple TV on Friday, November 13. Viewers can add Being Heumann to their watchlist on Apple TV .

Apple TV offers premium, compelling drama and comedy series, feature films, groundbreaking documentaries, and kids and family entertainment, and is available to watch across all of a user’s favorite screens. After its launch on November 1, 2019, Apple TV became the first all-original streaming service to launch around the world, and has premiered more original hits and received more award recognitions faster than any other streaming service in its debut. To date, Apple Original films, documentaries, and series have been honored with 919 wins and 3,829 award nominations and counting, including Academy Award Best Picture winner CODA and Academy Award winner F1, the highest-grossing sports feature of all time.

About Apple TV

Apple TV is available on the Apple TV app in 170 countries and regions, on over 1 billion screens, including iPhone; iPad; Apple TV 4K; Apple Vision Pro; Mac; popular smart TVs from Samsung, LG, Sony, VIZIO, TCL, and others; Roku and Amazon Fire TV devices; Chromecast with Google TV; PlayStation and Xbox gaming consoles; and at tv.apple.com , for $14.99 per month with a seven-day free trial for new subscribers. For a limited time, customers who purchase and activate a new iPhone, iPad, Apple TV 4K, or Mac can enjoy three months of Apple TV for free. 2

For more information, visit apple.com/tvpr and see the full list of supported devices .

es.title: Cadence Tactile Tablet, la pantalla táctil que permite explorar gráficos, braille y vídeo en tiempo real
es.summary: El acceso a la información digital sigue planteando importantes barreras para las personas ciegas y con discapacidad visual. Aunque las líneas braille y los lectores de pantalla han facilitado considerablemente el uso de ordenadores y dispositivos electrónicos, determinados contenidos, como gráficos, mapas, imágenes o vídeos, continúan siendo difíciles de explorar de forma autónoma. En este […] La entrada Cadence Tactile Tablet, la pantalla táctil que permite explorar gráficos, braille y vídeo en tiempo real se publicó primero en Conticgo .
es.body:
El acceso a la información digital sigue planteando importantes barreras para las personas ciegas y con discapacidad visual. Aunque las líneas braille y los lectores de pantalla han facilitado considerablemente el uso de ordenadores y dispositivos electrónicos, determinados contenidos, como gráficos, mapas, imágenes o vídeos, continúan siendo difíciles de explorar de forma autónoma.

En este contexto surge Cadence Tactile Tablet , un dispositivo desarrollado por la empresa estadounidense Tactile Engineering que propone una nueva forma de interactuar con los contenidos digitales: una pantalla táctil dinámica capaz de representar texto en braille, gráficos e incluso imágenes en movimiento.

A diferencia de las líneas braille tradicionales, que presentan los caracteres de forma secuencial en una única línea, Cadence incorpora una superficie formada por pequeños puntos móviles que pueden elevarse y descender para representar información mediante el tacto.

Su pantalla dispone de 384 puntos táctiles , distribuidos en 48 celdas braille de ocho puntos, organizadas en cuatro líneas de doce celdas. Esta configuración permite consultar varias líneas de texto simultáneamente y explorar representaciones gráficas sin depender exclusivamente de descripciones verbales.

El dispositivo utiliza tecnología MEMS ( Micro-Electro-Mechanical Systems ), basada en sistemas microelectromecánicos, para controlar el movimiento de los puntos táctiles. Según el fabricante, estos pueden actualizarse hasta tres veces por segundo, permitiendo modificar la información que aparece bajo los dedos.

Una de las características más llamativas de Cadence es su capacidad para representar gráficos táctiles dinámicos. Esto significa que la superficie no se limita a mostrar una imagen estática, sino que puede modificar los puntos en tiempo real para transmitir información cambiante.

Entre sus posibilidades destacan:

Una demostración especialmente llamativa tuvo lugar durante las 500 Millas de Indianápolis de 2026. Mediante Cadence, los aficionados ciegos pudieron seguir táctilmente el movimiento de los coches en el circuito, convirtiendo la información visual de la carrera en patrones que cambiaban bajo sus dedos.

Esta experiencia muestra cómo la tecnología táctil puede ampliar el acceso no solo a la lectura y al aprendizaje, sino también a acontecimientos deportivos y contenidos audiovisuales.

Otra de sus particularidades es su diseño modular. Cadence puede utilizarse como una unidad independiente o conectarse con otras unidades para ampliar la superficie táctil disponible.

El fabricante contempla configuraciones de hasta cuatro dispositivos conectados, que permiten trabajar con una superficie de mayor tamaño y representar contenidos más amplios.

Además, incorpora teclado braille tipo Perkins, controles direccionales y botones multifunción para navegar por los contenidos, seleccionar líneas, acceder a etiquetas y controlar diferentes aplicaciones.

La conexión con ordenadores y dispositivos compatibles se realiza mediante Bluetooth o USB-C. También dispone de software propio, CadenceOS, que permite gestionar el dispositivo y acceder a diferentes aplicaciones y contenidos.

Las aplicaciones de una pantalla táctil de estas características pueden ser especialmente interesantes en el ámbito educativo.

El acceso a mapas, gráficos matemáticos, representaciones científicas y otros recursos visuales constituye uno de los grandes retos de la educación inclusiva. Aunque existen materiales en relieve y herramientas de adaptación, su elaboración puede requerir tiempo, conocimientos especializados y recursos específicos.

Dispositivos como Cadence permiten explorar nuevas formas de presentar estos contenidos digitalmente, facilitando su actualización y ofreciendo posibilidades de interacción que no proporcionan los materiales táctiles estáticos.

También pueden contribuir al acceso a información que cambia constantemente, como gráficos estadísticos, retransmisiones deportivas o determinadas representaciones audiovisuales.

No obstante, es importante recordar que la disponibilidad de una pantalla táctil dinámica no garantiza por sí sola la accesibilidad de cualquier contenido. La distribución de los puntos, la complejidad de las representaciones y la necesidad de una adaptación comprensible siguen siendo aspectos fundamentales para que la información pueda interpretarse correctamente mediante el tacto.

Cadence Tactile Tablet representa una evolución interesante dentro de la tiflotecnología: pasar de dispositivos centrados principalmente en reproducir texto braille a superficies capaces de transmitir información espacial y dinámica.

Su desarrollo abre nuevas posibilidades para la lectura, la educación, la comunicación y el acceso a contenidos digitales. También plantea una cuestión importante de cara al futuro: cómo conseguir que las imágenes, los gráficos y otros contenidos diseñados originalmente para la vista puedan convertirse en experiencias táctiles realmente comprensibles y accesibles.

La tecnología todavía tiene retos por delante, pero propuestas como esta muestran que el futuro de la accesibilidad digital también pasa por ampliar las posibilidades del sentido del tacto.

Si te ha gustado esta noticia no te pierdas las últimas novedades en tiflotectnología en nuestro apartado de noticias y redes sociales .

Fuente: Tactile Engineering , Double Tap Live .

en.title: NoteTell Money Reader
en.summary: NoteTell Money Reader is designed to help people who are blind or have low vision identify bills in real time. Simply point the iPhone camera at the bill you want to identify, then hear, feel, or see its value. If you’re blind, have low vision, or are deafblind, NoteTell Money Reader lets you identify bills without any assistance. While shopping, use NoteTell to check your money at the checkout and make sure you get the right change back. You can also use NoteTell to quickly sort your money at home. NoteTell doesn’t require an internet connection, so it identifies bills anywhere, at any time. NoteTell can identify bills at any angle. It is designed to work with bills that are folded, creased, worn, or partly in view. NoteTell is designed to work indoors, outdoors, and even in total darkness. When your environment is too dark to identify bills, NoteTell turns the flashlight on automatically. Vibration Mode tells you the value of each bill as vibrations in your hand—without anyone else hearing it. Each bill has its own vibration pattern. The lowest bill has one pulse, and each higher bill has one more. Pulses come in pairs, so they’re easier to count. Vibration Mode is also useful in noisy places and for people who are deafblind. When VoiceOver is on, double-tap with two fingers to switch between Speech Mode and Vibration Mode. For users with low vision, NoteTell shows the value of each bill in large, high-contrast numbers on the screen. You can complete every task in NoteTell Money Reader using only VoiceOver, without sighted assistance. If you use a braille display with VoiceOver, you can use NoteTell to get the value of each bill in real time. Ask Siri, “Identify currency with NoteTell,” to use NoteTell hands-free. You can also add NoteTell to Control Center or the Lock Screen, assign it to the Action button, or set it up as a Vocal Shortcut. With the full version, you can use Currency Conversion to hear each bill’s value in your home currency when you travel. NoteTell uses on-device processing to identify bills, which means your data never leaves your iPhone. Camera images are never stored on the device or on any servers. You can try the full version free for 14 days. You won’t be charged when the trial ends. You can continue using NoteTell for free to identify the lowest notes of each currency. The full version is also available as a one-time purchase. And with Family Sharing, up to five other people can enjoy your purchase too.
