en.body:
ZoomText and Fusion are powerful accessibility tools designed for people with low vision. ZoomText is a screen magnifier and reader, while Fusion combines all of ZoomText’s features with the full JAWS screen reader, offering both magnification and speech.

Since October is National Disability Employment Awareness Month, we want to take this opportunity to spotlight powerful features of ZoomText and Fusion that will help you be more productive in the workplace. This blog series will run throughout October, with a new post every Thursday featuring helpful information and practical tips to make the most of ZoomText and Fusion as you work. To help you get started, we’ll highlight some of the most important ZoomText and Fusion features that can make your daily work tasks easier and more efficient.

ZoomText and Fusion offer flexible magnification , letting you choose the level that works best for your tasks and environment. You can select from different zoom window types —like full screen, lens, or docked—and even use multiple monitors for expanded workspace. Advanced Smoothing, including xFont and Geometric Smoothing, keeps text and graphics sharp and easy to read at any magnification level.

Color Enhancements allow you to adjust color settings for better clarity. You can apply preset color schemes, switch to two-color modes, or replace specific problem colors to make on-screen content easier to see. These options help reduce eye strain, especially during long workdays.

Focus enhancements help you track your position in menus, dialogs, and application controls, so you never lose your place. Mouse pointers and cursors can be customized in size and color, making them easier to spot and follow on the screen.

AppReader is a built-in tool that reads documents, web pages, and emails aloud, supporting users who need to hear text read aloud. This is extremely useful for users who experience eye fatigue when reading long documents and emails.

For Fusion users, the full JAWS screen reader is included, adding speech and Braille support to all ZoomText magnification features. JAWS features like Say All (which reads from your cursor position), virtual cursor navigation for web pages and applications, and Quick Navigation keys for navigating web pages make workplace tasks more accessible. Fusion lets you switch seamlessly between magnification and speech, depending on your needs.

With ZoomText and Fusion, you can customize your environment to match your vision needs and adjust settings at any time as your tasks change. You can also save your personalized settings, so your preferred setup is always ready whenever you start your work day.

Stay tuned for Week 2, where we’ll explore how to use ZoomText and Fusion across your workday, from Microsoft Word to Teams, to help you stay productive and connected. We’ll discuss important ZoomText and Fusion settings, plus provide tips for navigating workplace apps with more confidence and ease.

Have questions? Email training@vispero.com .

en.title: iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max Review: I Keep Coming Back to the Pro
en.summary: The last couple years have been big for iPhone. In 2025, Apple introduced two brand new iPhone models: iPhone 16e, an entry-level model with most of the essential components of the more expensive iPhones of its generation; and iPhone Air, the thinnest-ever iPhone to date at the time. This year, Apple announced the iPhone Duo, the company's first-ever foldable iPhone and with it, a whole new form factor and way of using iPhone as we know it. In between the new iPhone models, Apple has, year-by-year, continued the steady evolution of its Pro and Pro Max phones. This year, for the first time, I had the opportunity to review both iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max. One of the devices was a review unit on loan from Apple, whilst the other was the phone I purchased for myself. Being able to use both devices, one after the other, gave me a unique opportunity to evaluate them side-by-side, and I have a much deeper appreciation for each model and its strengths (and limitations). And after spending time with each phone, I came away with a surprising and yet inevitable conclusion: while iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max are similar, they are very different devices for very different use cases. And only one of them is a device I would routinely recommend for most people. Getting a Feel for iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max On the surface, iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max are almost identical to last year's devices. Cosmic Orange is out in favor of Burgundy and Glacier [light blue], but on the outside at least, not much else has changed. iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max come in Black, Silver, Glacier [light blue], and Burgundy. Both devices have a Super Retina XDR display with Ceramic Shield 2; forged unibody featuring an Apple-designed 7000 series aluminum alloy; and a color-matched glass back with Ceramic Shield. iPhone 18 Pro has a 6.3-inch display, while the display on iPhone 18 Pro Max is 6.9 inches. (Displays are measured diagonally.) The left edge of the device houses the Action Button and, below that, the Volume Buttons. The right edge of the device has the Side Button at the top and the Camera Control towards the bottom. The bottom edge of iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max holds the bottom speaker on the left, a USB-C port in the middle, and the microphone on the right. There are three different cameras on the top back of the device, housed in the plateau. The plateau extends across approximately the top third of the back of the device. The back glass feels very similar in texture to the forged unibody. In my hand—that all-important ‘hand-feel’—iPhone 18 Pro feels, as Goldilocks would say, ‘just right’. It is appropriately heavy—‘substantial’—and is neither so big such that holding it one-handed is likely to be difficult for most; nor is it so small that one must compromise on battery life or overall form and function. Whereas iPhone 18 Pro feels ideal for most, iPhone 18 Pro Max is absolutely huge in comparison and almost feels unwieldy. It is heavy in the hand and even heavier in the pocket of my khakis. One-handed usage is not really an option, though if you are already used to and comfortable with the Pro Max phones, do note that iPhone 18 Pro Max has not changed in size. Battery Life iPhone 18 Pro offers up to 36 hours of video playback with up to 24 hours of typical usage per charge, while iPhone 18 Pro Max offers up to 45 hours of video playback and up to 30 hours of typical usage per charge. In my experience, battery life on even the smaller iPhone 18 Pro has been enough to get me through the day, and then some. On a typical day, I finished with around 40% battery remaining on iPhone 18 Pro and 60% on iPhone 18 Pro Max, give or take. The lowest I got the iPhone 18 Pro was 21% on my very first full day with the device, and the lowest I got the 18 Pro Max was 32% on a day when, unbeknownst to me, screen brightness got set to 100% and Screen Curtain became disabled. Not counting the days when the erroneous settings were a factor, my next-lowest end-of-day battery reading on iPhone 18 Pro Max was 46% after a little over 18 hours off the charger. On one day with exceptionally light usage, I finished at 64% with iPhone 18 Pro and 81% with iPhone 18 Pro Max. Performance iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max both share Apple’s latest and greatest A20 Pro processor and an improved cooling system. While I do not use my phones for processor-intensive work, what I can say is that day-to-day performance of the A20 Pro is as good as you could possibly want it to be. Apps and screens open quickly, and the operating system runs well. VoiceOver—Apple’s built-in screen reader for blind, DeafBlind, and low vision users—responds as soon as I touch the screen. There is no latency whatsoever. When compared to last year’s A19 Pro, in day-to-day device usage, I noticed hardly any difference with this year's A20 Pro in iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max. The A19 series of processors already ran iOS 27 and VoiceOver exceptionally well, with Apple definitely appearing to have done some serious work to make VoiceOver feel more snappy. Usually, when one installs a new major update, there is a small decrease in VoiceOver responsiveness; this was not the case for me this year running iOS 27 on iPhone 17 Pro Max. (I also tested several of the iOS 27 betas on an iPhone 17e with the regular A19 processor, and my experience was the same.) Given that performance of the A19 Pro was already incredibly good in everyday usage, it should come as no surprise then that this year’s A20 Pro is only nominally better for the same types of work. It is hard to improve on excellent, but companies of course will (and should) try. In terms of device heat, I cannot honestly say that I noticed any huge reduction in heat under load between iPhone 17 Pro Max and this year's models, except on my first couple days with iPhone 18 Pro. Comparing between iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max, iPhone 18 Pro did anecdotally seem to be more prone to getting warmer quicker, though that extra warmth may have been caused by a particular third-party app. Speakers and Sound When I shared my initial impressions of iPhone 18 Pro ahead of the launch, I wrote about how much I liked the sound from the device’s speaker. My week with the device confirmed my initial experience: whether listening to VoiceOver or music, the speakers on iPhone 18 Pro sound full, warm, balanced, and are all around a joy to listen to. iPhone 18 Pro Max is a bit more of a mixed bag. Compared to iPhone 18 Pro, the speakers on iPhone 18 Pro Max have much more bass, more high end, and... Less of the midrange warmth that makes the iPhone 18 Pro sound so good overall. Going from iPhone 18 Pro to iPhone 18 Pro Max, I was, honestly, disappointed. It's not all bad, though. While my primary point of reference for speaker quality is VoiceOver speech and other spoken audio, the very things that make iPhone 18 Pro Max sound so poor with spoken audio are what make it stand out with music. When listening to music, iPhone 18 Pro Max outshines the smaller iPhone 18 Pro: there is more bass, more high end, and certainly more volume. While I wouldn't say that the sound is room-filling by any stretch of the imagination, it is quite loud at close range and more than enough to replace a small Bluetooth speaker. Siri AI While not specifically a new feature of this year's iPhones, Siri got a major upgrade in iOS 27. Since updating, I find myself using Siri a lot more for things I would have previously needed to use a third-party description app or AI service for. Asking research-based questions is an obvious one, but it goes beyond that. For example, whilst waiting for the arrival of my Apple Watch Series 12, I asked Siri to tell me where the delivery was on the map. I have also used Siri AI to describe weather graphics posted on Facebook, which is especially helpful as Siri AI can access my contextual information that Apple's Intelligent Image Descriptions or third-party tools cannot. "Where is that line of thunderstorms relative to me?" is a question that Siri AI can answer with access to my location, and I find the descriptions of what's onscreen to be sufficiently detailed and helpful. And yet, Siri AI is not as good as it could be. My experiences using AI services like ChatGPT to vibecode and do other tasks using natural language sometimes left me disappointed with Siri AI. Since Siri AI is integrated right into the operating system, it should be able to do everything that I can accomplish through navigating the UI manually. And so far at least, this has not been the case. Camera, Cellular, and Other Things One of the headline new features of iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max is the 48MP Fusion Main camera with variable aperture. Being blind, I am not able to speak firsthand to this and, while I had a very interesting discussion with ChatGPT on variable aperture and what this might mean in practical terms, I am not comfortable including any of that here as I cannot independently verify its accuracy. For an in-depth evaluation of the iPhone 18 Pro camera specifically, I recommend this review by PetaPixel's Jaron Schneider. iPhone 18 Pro (specifically) has the Apple C2 modem, and both models have the Apple N1 wireless networking chip. In my speed tests, the only meaningful difference between the C2 modem in iPhone 18 Pro and the modem in iPhone 18 Pro Max was that the C2 on iPhone 18 Pro seemed to deliver upload speeds that were slightly faster. Testing was done on the T-Mobile network in Chicago. As spotted by AppleVis user Zach M, iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max support 8-dot braille in Braille Screen Input (BSI), and calibration of braille dots in BSI now works similar to how it is on iPad. Not being familiar with 8-dot braille, I cannot speak to this firsthand. Due to the size of its battery, iPhone 18 Pro Max has a "Prepare to Ship" option that one must use to sufficiently discharge the battery and limit battery capacity prior to shipping it for repair or any other reason. This Apple Support Article has more info. With a compatible adapter, iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max can charge up to 50% in 15 minutes. While I do not think I have the prerequisite adapter for this, my own subjective experience is that charging is faster than on last year's model. Which Phone Should I Buy? As I see it, my role as a reviewer is to evaluate a phone and make purchasing recommendations in terms of how I think most people are likely to use it; rather than assessing based on my own preferences which are very specific and unique to me. As such, you may have noticed that up to this point, I have tried to keep my opinions focused on what I feel are the strengths and weaknesses of each device (rather than what "I" like in a phone). This was intentional. My goal in my reviews is to give you information and let you come to your own conclusions. Complicating any attempt at a meaningful recommendation that will withstand the test of time is that we are just beginning the 2026-27 iPhone release cycle, with more releases likely on the way throughout the next six or so months. iPhone Duo is going to be available for preorder next week, with customer availability beginning October 23. The more I learn about and consider iPhone Duo, the more I am realizing that it is going to be unlike anything we have seen before. iPhone Duo is something completely new, with a new form factor and user experience. Watch this space. With all of that in mind, I think that iPhone 18 Pro is likely to be the best iPhone for most people in the 2026-27 cycle. The size of iPhone 18 Pro is 'just right', and the battery will likely get you through the day (if not more). Performance is equally good no matter which model you choose. And while the speakers on iPhone 18 Pro Max definitely have more bass and high end, iPhone 18 Pro sounds better and more natural overall, and it is the device I would myself prefer to listen to long-term. Of course, there are some people for whom iPhone 18 Pro Max is an easy recommendation. If like me you want the absolute best battery life possible, iPhone 18 Pro Max is the only phone to get. Likewise, iPhone 18 Pro Max is also a strong contender for people with low vision, though the iPhone Duo I think will be the winner in that category with its 7.6-inch inner display. I just would not recommend iPhone 18 Pro Max for someone whose top priority is sound quality of VoiceOver or other spoken audio, or if you value being able to hold and use your device easily in one hand. If you want a new iPhone but the 18 Pro/Max and Duo are not in your budget, consider that Apple has over the last couple years released budget-oriented iPhone models in the early part of the year. If the past couple years are any indicator, these devices will likely include a current-generation A20-series processor, so day-to-day performance will likely be on par with the Pro/Max and Duo for everyday use. When buying a new iPhone, there are a couple of things I would actively caution you against. First, I would not recommend buying an older iPhone model (including the currently available iPhone Air, iPhone 17, and iPhone 17e), as these devices have older processors. While software support on older devices is very good (iOS 27, for example, will run on the 2019 iPhone 11 series), Apple has historically ended software support one processor generation at a time. Put another way: an iPhone 18 is likely to get one more year of software updates than is the iPhone 17 series and original iPhone Air, as these devices have last year's A19-series processors. The other thing I encourage caution with is carrier iPhone promos. While these programs can provide great-looking offers up front, I am of the opinion that carrier promos are primarily meant to benefit the carrier and keep the customer locked in and paying. If buying from your carrier, make sure the math works out and it really is in your best interest. Depending on your location, Apple may offer financing and upgrade options, so you could buy on installments directly from Apple and avoid your carrier entirely. Lastly, if you want a refurbished iPhone, stick to devices certified refurbished by Apple. If you buy a refurbished device from Apple, you are guaranteed a certain level of quality that you may not easily find on the used market. Conclusion On the day I published this review, I did something surprising: I transferred all of my data and my cellular plans back onto iPhone 18 Pro. As much as I love the battery life of iPhone 18 Pro Max, I kept being drawn back to iPhone 18 Pro for its size, form factor, 'holdability', and great-sounding speakers. While my personal preference is and will always be for the phone with the largest battery, iPhone 18 Pro really is, I think, the best iPhone for most people this year. I really do like it.

When buying a new iPhone, there are a couple of things I would actively caution you against. First, I would not recommend buying an older iPhone model (including the currently available iPhone Air, iPhone 17, and iPhone 17e), as these devices have older processors. While software support on older devices is very good (iOS 27, for example, will run on the 2019 iPhone 11 series), Apple has historically ended software support one processor generation at a time. Put another way: an iPhone 18 is likely to get one more year of software updates than is the iPhone 17 series and original iPhone Air, as these devices have last year's A19-series processors.

The other thing I encourage caution with is carrier iPhone promos. While these programs can provide great-looking offers up front, I am of the opinion that carrier promos are primarily meant to benefit the carrier and keep the customer locked in and paying. If buying from your carrier, make sure the math works out and it really is in your best interest. Depending on your location, Apple may offer financing and upgrade options, so you could buy on installments directly from Apple and avoid your carrier entirely.

Lastly, if you want a refurbished iPhone, stick to devices certified refurbished by Apple. If you buy a refurbished device from Apple, you are guaranteed a certain level of quality that you may not easily find on the used market.

On the day I published this review, I did something surprising: I transferred all of my data and my cellular plans back onto iPhone 18 Pro. As much as I love the battery life of iPhone 18 Pro Max, I kept being drawn back to iPhone 18 Pro for its size, form factor, 'holdability', and great-sounding speakers. While my personal preference is and will always be for the phone with the largest battery, iPhone 18 Pro really is, I think, the best iPhone for most people this year. I really do like it.

es.title: Ya disponible la cuarta beta de NVDA 2026.3
es.summary: Tal y como ha anunciado NV Access mediante esta publicación, la beta 4 de NVDA 2026.3 ya se encuentra disponible para descarga y pruebas. Si quieres saber qué ofrece la próxima versión de NVDA antes de que se libere oficialmente, no dudes en descargar esta beta y proporcionar comentarios por los canales de la comunidad, … Continuar leyendo "Ya disponible la cuarta beta de NVDA 2026.3" La entrada Ya disponible la cuarta beta de NVDA 2026.3 se publicó primero en NVDA en español .
es.body:
Tal y como ha anunciado NV Access mediante esta publicación , la beta 4 de NVDA 2026.3 ya se encuentra disponible para descarga y pruebas. Si quieres saber qué ofrece la próxima versión de NVDA antes de que se libere oficialmente, no dudes en descargar esta beta y proporcionar comentarios por los canales de la comunidad, o por el sistema de informe de fallos de NV Access . Esta versión no es apta para entornos de producción. Al instalar esta beta te unirás al canal beta, y sólo recibirás avisos de actualización de compilaciones beta y candidatas a liberación (rc). El canal beta/rc siempre te mantendrá al día con la versión más reciente de NVDA. La última rc de un ciclo de liberación es idéntica a la última versión estable. Para regresar al canal de versiones estables, instala a mano la última versión estable.

Esta versión incorpora importantes mejoras de rendimiento, mejoras en los diálogos de NVDA, y entrada expandida por la pantalla táctil. Se han hecho varias mejoras para reducir los retrasos y aumentar el rendimiento. Ahora NVDA recupera y captura más información sobre los controles en segundo plano, mejorando el rendimiento en controles como cuadros combinados y el explorador de archivos. NVDA ya no hace que se rompan el explorador de archivos u otras aplicaciones al cerrarlo o reiniciarlo. NVDA se recupera ahora más rápido cuando una aplicación deja de responder, y ya no se colgará ni inundará el registro con errores en aplicaciones que no responden. En regiones vivas de texto, como las terminales, NVDA ya no se cuelga cuando se vuelcan en pantalla importantes cantidades de texto. Se han añadido menús de contexto y atajos de teclado a los diálogos de perfiles de configuración, gestos de entrada y diccionarios del habla, haciendo que estos diálogos sean más fáciles de usar con el teclado. Ahora también es posible cambiar directamente un gesto existente en el diálogo Gestos de entrada. Se ha modernizado el diálogo que presenta mensajes explorables y ahora soporta mejor cambiar su tamaño, maximizarlo y minimizarlo. Se ha expandido significativamente la entrada por pantalla táctil. Los gestos de dos deslizamientos secuenciales ahora combinan dos deslizamientos en rápida sucesión en un solo gesto, incrementando enormemente la cantidad de gestos asociables. También se soportan ahora los gestos de borde, permitiendo que los gestos que comiencen a 15 mm de cualquier borde de la pantalla se asocien independientemente de los mismos gestos realizados en el centro de la pantalla. Se ha añadido una nueva orden sin asignar para mover el cursor del ratón al centro de la vista ampliada. Se puede usar el OCR de Windows con la lupa o la cortina de pantalla activadas. Se ha actualizado Liblouis con nuevas tablas braille en Elfdaliano, sami, maorí, braille unificado inglés de Nueva Zelanda, y aitiano criollo, una tabla noruega para texto en español, y variantes adicionales de sueco de 6 y 8 puntos. Se ha actualizado Espeak NG añadiendo soporte para liguriano y abkhaz. Para instalar esta beta, puedes configurar el canal «rc y beta» en el complemento Selector del canal de actualización y buscar actualizaciones desde el menú Ayuda de NVDA, o actualizar desde una beta anterior. Y como siempre, también puedes descargar manualmente el instalador de NVDA 2026.3 beta 4 . Su suma de comprobación SHA256, que te permitirá garantizar la integridad del archivo descargado, es 8be91476179710c4abffe5094459df9be1696d92e5d6cd0ace47d52321bb87ab. ¡Feliz martes!

La entrada Ya disponible la cuarta beta de NVDA 2026.3 se publicó primero en NVDA en español .

es.body:
Disponible el número 50 de “Arroba Sonora”, el podcast de tecnología del CTI, que puede descargarse desde el Gestor ONCE de Libros Digitales, el ClubONCE o escucharse a través de las principales plataformas de podcast o desde la Web del CTI.

En este número, con el que “Arroba Sonora” alcanza su edición número 50, se comienza repasando las principales novedades en materia de accesibilidad que incorpora iOS 27 . Se analizarán algunas de las nuevas funciones y mejoras que pueden resultar de especial interés para las personas con ceguera o deficiencia visual grave, así como otros cambios relacionados con la accesibilidad y el uso de los dispositivos de Apple.

A continuación, se presenta TagFit , una aplicación pensada para etiquetar y organizar productos. Durante el episodio se explicará en qué consiste esta herramienta, cuáles son sus principales funcionalidades y de qué manera puede facilitar la identificación, clasificación y organización de distintos productos en el día a día.

También se ofrece una comparativa de las aplicaciones móviles de diferentes cadenas de supermercados e hipermercados para realizar la compra. Se analizarán sus principales características y, especialmente, su grado de accesibilidad y facilidad de uso para las personas con ceguera o deficiencia visual grave, prestando atención a aspectos como la navegación, la identificación de productos, la gestión de la cesta y el proceso de compra.

La edición se completa con la presentación del chatbot de Aena para WhatsApp , una herramienta que permite consultar información relacionada con vuelos y aeropuertos a través de esta popular aplicación de mensajería. Se explicará su funcionamiento y las posibilidades que ofrece para obtener información útil antes y durante un viaje.

El contenido íntegro de “Arroba Sonora” en formato texto puede descargarse desde el Gestor ONCE de Libros Digitales, o consultarse en la sección correspondiente de “Arroba Sonora” dentro de la Web del CTI.

en.title: In-Process 28th September 2026
en.summary: Let’s talk about NVDA 2026.3! NVDA 2026.3 Beta 2 Changes to the Changes Our International Communities Copying last spoken text Talking about NVDA Show Screen Overview NVDA 2026.3 Beta 2 As mentioned last edition, we released NVDA 2026.2 and dived straight into the beta period for NVDA 2026.3. Firstly, do go back and read all… Read More
en.body:
Let’s talk about NVDA 2026.3!

As mentioned last edition, we released NVDA 2026.2 and dived straight into the beta period for NVDA 2026.3 . Firstly, do go back and read all about NVDA 2026.2 if needed, but otherwise, let’s dive into what is coming up in NVDA 2026.3:

This release includes significant performance improvements, improvements to NVDA’s dialogs, and expanded touch screen input.

Several performance improvements have been made to reduce lag and improve responsiveness. NVDA now fetches and caches more information about controls in the background, improving performance in controls such as combo boxes and File Explorer. NVDA no longer causes File Explorer or other applications to crash when NVDA is exited or restarted. NVDA now recovers more quickly when an application stops responding, and will no longer freeze or flood the log with errors from unresponsive applications. In live text regions, such as terminals, NVDA no longer freezes when substantial amounts of text are dumped to the screen.

Context menus and keyboard shortcuts have been added to the Configuration Profiles, Input Gestures, and Speech Dictionaries dialogs, making these dialogs easier to use with the keyboard. It is also now possible to change an existing gesture directly in the Input Gestures dialog. The dialog used to present browsable messages has been modernized and now better supports resizing, maximizing, and minimizing.

Touch screen input has been significantly expanded. Sequential two-flick gestures now combine two flicks in quick succession into a single gesture, greatly increasing the number of bindable touch gestures. Edge gestures are also now supported, allowing gestures that begin within 15 mm of any screen edge to be bound independently from the same gesture performed in the centre of the screen.

A new unassigned command has been added to move the mouse cursor to the centre of the magnified view. Windows OCR can now be used while the Screen Curtain or NVDA’s built-in Magnifier is active.

Liblouis has been updated with new Elfdalian, Sami, Maori, New Zealand Unified English Braille, and Haitian Creole braille tables, a Norwegian table for Spanish text, and additional Swedish 6 and 8 dot variants. eSpeak NG has been updated with added support for Ligurian and Abkhaz.

Updates to translations Fix bug with Magnifier’s “Show screen overview” feature when using relative tracking mode Updated eSpeak In browse mode, alt+upArrow and alt+downArrow now collapse or expand combo boxes in more situations Prevent flashing from shifting magnifier colour filters to reduce seizure risk Update to the Chinese Word Segmentation library cppjieba to fix startup crashes from Chinese paths

If you’ve looked at the changes document for the NVDA 2026.3 betas , you might have noticed a change to the formatting. Or rather, some new formatting. Instead of having a list of features, and then breaking that up into sub-lists of Braille features and Touch Screen features and Browse mode features, we’ve made them headings:

“What’s new in NVDA” is at the top of the document and is a heading level 1 – press shift+1 to jump back to that from anywhere (or control+home since it’s at the top of the document). The version of NVDA, “2026.3”, “2026.2” etc, is a heading level 2. Press 2 to jump to the next older version of NVDA, or shift+2 to jump back to the start of the current version, or next newest version of NVDA. “New features”, “Changes”, “Bug Fixes”, “Changes for Developers”, “Security fixes”, and “Important notes” are all Heading level 3. sub-headings in the section, new features, changes, etc, are heading level 4. In the “New Features” for NVDA 2026.3 for instance, press 4 to jump to “Braille”, “Touch Screen Input”, “Browse Mode”, which are all sections of new features for this version.

If you are used to simply arrowing down through the list and reading each feature, that still works as it did. Or if you press i to jump between list items, that will still work, although you will miss the heading. If you navigate like that and hear “List with x items” and you’re not sure what the list is, press shift+h to jump to the previous heading (at any level) and it will move to the heading just before the list. As something new, we’re interested in what you think – good or bad. It’s the first time we’ve changed the formatting in awhile (though not the first at all, though the last change will not have been as noticeable to all our users).

While we’ve been sprucing things up, we recently gave the “ Connect with the NVDA Community ” page a once over. Firstly, we made sure all the links worked and followed up those with problems. As a result of that, we’ve removed a couple in consultation with their owners (Finnish and Swedish particularly) and added a couple more we had found along the way (Hi to our friends from the Brazilian Portuguese site!)

We also took the opportunity to add headings at H3 for each language, so you can jump or link to the Romanian resources directly now.

We’re always interested in adding new resources to the list. Are you aware of any other groups we’re not aware of? Particularly in languages not yet listed there. Please get in touch if you know of any.

One of the popular features in NVDA 2026.2 was the addition of NVDA+x to repeat the last spoken information. You could press that twice quickly to have the information displayed in a dialog so you could read it with more granular control. If what you want to do is copy the information, while you can do it from that dialog, we’ve added a new command to NVDA 2026.3 to make it even easier. Press NVDA+control+x to copy the last spoken information directly to the clipboard. Thank you to community contributor Cary for his work on this feature!

(A screenshot of the original NVDA+x double press dialog, showing the new feature bullet point for the NVDA+control+x command. Note the dialog has white text on black, because I had the magnifier running with colours inverted when I took the screenshot.)

We love talking about NVDA! I often forget to mention interviews here, but we’ve recently done a couple I thought I’d share:

Access Point Firstly, our “Access Point” collaboration with World Services for the Blind continues with the second in our podcast series, on everything new in NVDA 2026.2.

Tek Talk Next, Training & Support Manager Quentin was on Tek Talk , again covering everything new with NVDA.

And, on a slightly different topic NOT involving us talking – but if YOU love talking about NVDA, accessibility and navigation, Monash University, in Australia, are offering a paid PhD Scholarship in Communication and Navigation for Blind and Low Vision People .

Monash are looking for a linguist or researcher with a related background to investigate how Blind and Low Vision people navigate the world using technology.

The project focuses on video ethnography, multimodal communication, and users’ experiences of navigation technology, with opportunities to collaborate with researchers in assistive technology and AI.

This is open to both Australians and International applicants It’s also part of the Monash Assistive Technology and Society Centre (MATS) and Monash AI Institute so the successful applicant will have lots of opportunity to collaborate with technologists about building better navigational tech going forward.

Do refer to the position description at Monash for all the details.

One of the features of the magnifier we didn’t mention much last time is the Show Entire Screen Overview. Since one of the fixes in the latest NVDA 2026.3 beta is a fix involving this feature, I thought it was worth a mention. So firstly, the fix is that it WILL now work if using relative tracking mode – so if you prefer that magnifier tracking mode, you might want to upgrade before trying it out.

With the magnifier running, press NVDA+shift+L to “Show entire screen”. This temporarily zooms out to show the whole screen (as if the magnifier wasn’t running). After a couple of seconds without the mouse moving, the view zooms back in again.

Because the view smoothly zooms out and then back in again, it makes it easier to tell where the zoomed area is in relation to the whole screen. By waiting for mouse movement to stop, it allows a user to explore the unmagnified view and then smoothly zooms in to where the focus currently is.

If you wish to instantly enable or disable the magnifier, NVDA+shift+w will do this immediately, without zoom out (and then only magnifies again once you press NVDA+shift+w again).

Another difference is that pressing NVDA+shift+L zooms out but leaves any colour filtering enabled. If you wish to quickly zoom out and remove colour filtering, then you may find turning off the magnifier ( NVDA+shift+w ) works better.

And a related tip – if you don’t want magnification BUT do want colour filtering, you can enable the magnifier, enable colour filtering ( NVDA+shift+i ) and then zoom out to 1x ( NVDA+shift+minus ).

That’s all for this week. A little longer than it sometimes is, but there we covered quite a few keystrokes – did you learn any new ones? Surely at least NVDA+control+x ? Do try out the latest 2026.3 beta, and some of those commands. Do please keep giving feedback on the changes and improvements. Also please do share any other international communities we aren’t yet aware of.

es.title: Accesibilidad y Tecnología Vive el fútbol accesible con Movistar Touch en el estadio Riyadh Air Metropolitano.
es.summary: Gracias a la colaboración entre la ONCE, Movistar y el Atlético de Madrid, las personas afiliadas podrán disfrutar de una experiencia más accesible e inmersiva durante los partidos de fútbol que se celebren en el estadio Riyadh Air Metropolitano.
es.body:
Gracias a la colaboración entre la ONCE, Movistar y el Atlético de Madrid, las personas afiliadas podrán disfrutar de una experiencia más accesible e inmersiva durante los partidos de fútbol que se celebren en el estadio Riyadh Air Metropolitano.

Se trata de Movistar Touch , un servicio gratuito dirigido a aficionados con entrada para el encuentro, que permite seguir el desarrollo del partido mediante audiodescripción y una tableta háptica capaz de reproducir en tiempo real la posición del balón sobre el terreno de juego. Esta tecnología ofrece una nueva forma de vivir la emoción del fútbol y constituye un excelente ejemplo de cómo la innovación puede contribuir a derribar barreras y favorecer la participación de todas las personas.

Actualmente, el Riyadh Air Metropolitano es el único estadio de España que ofrece este sistema. Las personas afiliadas interesadas en utilizarlo deberán solicitarlo previamente enviando un correo electrónico a inclusion@atleticodemadrid.com , indicando el partido de LALIGA para el que desean adquirir entradas y hacer uso del servicio.

Es importante tener en cuenta que Movistar Touch dispone de un número limitado de unidades, por lo que se recomienda realizar la solicitud con la mayor antelación posible.

Esta iniciativa se enmarca en la colaboración que el Atlético de Madrid mantiene desde hace años con la ONCE y Fundación ONCE para seguir mejorando la accesibilidad de sus instalaciones y servicios, reforzando así su compromiso con un deporte más inclusivo y accesible para todos.

en.title: In-Process 8th September 2026
en.summary: It’s a busy and exciting time – it’s release time! Let’s dive in and see what’s new: NVDA 2026.2 Magnifier A new Beta already? Resetting to Factory Defaults NVDA 2026.2 NVDA 2026.2 has been released! This release includes a new built-in Magnifier feature, improvements to touch gestures and navigation, and expanded speech and braille capabilities.… Read More
en.body:
It’s a busy and exciting time – it’s release time! Let’s dive in and see what’s new:

NVDA 2026.2 has been released ! This release includes a new built-in Magnifier feature, improvements to touch gestures and navigation, and expanded speech and braille capabilities.

The Magnifier provides zoom and color filtering options to assist users with visual impairments. The Magnifier currently only supports full screen mode, with docked modes planned in a future release. Touch support has been significantly expanded with new pinch gestures and touch-based browse mode navigation for web content. You can now navigate between links, headings, form fields, and other elements using touch flicks.

Speech features have been enhanced with support for custom speech dictionaries that can be provided by add-ons and new dictionary entry types for more granular control. A new voice setting for OneCore voices was added to control pauses after punctuation. A new command allows repeating the last spoken information, with the ability to display it in a browsable message. The default gesture to repeat the last spoken information is NVDA+x , which can be changed in the Input Gestures dialog.

The braille display can now automatically scroll, and DotPad devices support multi-button combinations. The default gesture to toggle automatic scroll is NVDA+alt+k .

Liblouis has been updated with new Italian and Estonian braille tables. When resetting NVDA to factory defaults, an Undo button is now available to restore the previous configuration.

Download the new version from the NVDA 2026.2 release post (or by checking for updates from within NVDA).

As well as the article below, and a new extensive section on the magnifier in the User Guide, our “Basic Training for NVDA” module has been updated with a number of updates. Of particular interest is a new section on the magnifier, there is also a topic covering reading the last spoken information and other new and improved content. These new updates are currently only available in the electronic text version. You can purchase Basic Training for NVDA from our shop . If you have already purchased the module, you can download the new version with the Magnifier section from the downloads page after logging into your NV Access account .

We are very excited to incorporate a magnifier into NVDA for the first time. We have had a lot of comments from users who are excited for this feature, and we’ve had some questions too, so let’s cover off some of the things it can and cannot do, and why it is a useful addition to NVDA:

First Release Firstly, it’s worth highlighting that this is the first release of NVDA with a magnifier and so the features will improve over time. We try to ship NVDA features incrementally, keeping the initial design scope small and allowing for early user feedback. This allows us to grow the magnifier in response to user reaction. Currently NVDA only works as a full-screen magnifier. We plan to extend the options in future releases. Adding windowed / docked modes is a high priority once bugs are addressed and the full-screen mode is more polished.

What CAN the magnifier do? The magnifier has most of the features you might expect from such a feature: You can zoom in and out (from 1x up to 50x) The view will follow the mouse, keyboard focus, browse mode focus and NVDA navigator object and review cursor – user selectable You can pan the view with the keyboard, in configurable increments, or jump to the edges of the screen You can adjust the colours (normal, inverted or greyscale) You can choose how objects are tracked (Centred or relative to their position on screen) You can configure the keystrokes for the various functions There is a keystroke to briefly zoom out and show an overview of the screen

We have made a short demo of the magnification feature on our YouTube channel .

Should I change magnifiers? Particularly if you currently use another magnification solution, we very much encourage you to try out the NVDA magnifier. We are interested in your feedback, and particularly where you would like to see our feature improve.

If you already use Windows magnifier or another program, you can keep using it and it will continue to work with NVDA’s speech functions. Just as we don’t recommend having two screen readers running at once, we also wouldn’t recommend having NVDA’s magnifier AND another magnifier running at the same time.

If you do currently use Windows Magnifier, some of the reasons you may consider NVDA’s magnifier: It starts when NVDA starts (once you enable it) Configurable keystrokes Greyscale colour filtering mode Relative tracking mode Ability to follow NVDA’s object navigation and review cursor Keys to jump to edges of screen No settings window always on screen Ability to set your desired settings once and save to a portable copy you can use on any computer

If you use Windows magnifier in docked or lens mode, or some of the other features which haven’t yet made it into the NVDA magnifier in NVDA 2026.2, then you may wish to stay with Windows magnifier for now – but we do encourage you to try out the NVDA magnifier and let us know what you think.

Before we even got this edition of In-Process finished, to tell you all about 2026.2…. we ALREADY have a new beta? Of NVDA 2026.3 ? Yep! And I’m not going to talk about that yet – if you want to check it out, please head to the beta release announcement . What I did want to briefly mention, was how we came to have a new beta out, when the paint isn’t even dry on NVDA 2026.2?

Great question! And it comes down to how we develop software. Both our internal developers, and the community are constantly working on improving features, fixing bugs, and adding new things into NVDA. As a new piece of code gets incorporated into NVDA, it goes into an “Alpha” build – an early pre-release build with whatever has been changed recently. This lets our developers and our most dedicated testers try it out and give feedback. These come out almost daily (and sometimes several in one day). Because of the quick turnaround, we don’t share them on social media or here on the blog, but if you’d like to try them out, alpha builds are publicly available from the snapshots page . Be aware that they may not be as polished as the stable releases – though the process to test them out is identical.

So, generally a week after a stable release, we collate all the things which have been in alpha for at least a couple of weeks, and put them together into a “beta” release of the next version. While we may still have some features we are working on for later betas, as well any regressions or major issues discovered from the previous release, we can turn much of our development attention on towards the NEXT release.

So, if you ever find an issue with NVDA, the sooner you let us know, the sooner we can prioritise it and work on a fix as needed.

One of the perhaps less glamourous updates in NVDA 2026.2 is to a feature you hopefully don’t ever need to use.

“When resetting NVDA to factory defaults, an Undo button is now available to restore the previous configuration”

We’ve covered resetting NVDA to factory defaults previously , though it is worth being aware of. While something you hopefully don’t need, if you ever DO need it, it’s good to know it exists. With this new change, if you reset NVDA to factory defaults, a dialog appears advising “Your configuration has been reset to factory defaults. Choose OK to keep factory defaults, or Undo to restore your previous configuration”. This could be useful just in case you ever inadvertently activate the wrong item on the NVDA menu for instance, and may hopefully save you from needing go through setting up NVDA to your preferences again.

That’s all for this week, do update to NVDA 2026.2 if you haven’t already, and we’d love to hear your feedback on the new features – the magnifier of course, but also the other updates.

Bastón plegable ultraligero y muy fino, formado por seis elementos, muy cómodo para guardar en bolsillos y bolsos debido a sus reducidas dimensiones una vez plegado. Está realizado en aluminio de alta resistencia y pintado en blanco. Dispone de empuñadura de caucho ergonómica y contera giratoria.

Enzo vive con su familia en Erizona, una preciosa montaña donde habitan muchas familias de erizos. Un día, la señora Aguja, una amiga de su madre, pasa por su madriguera a visitarlos. Al marcharse, quiere que Enzo le dé un beso y un abrazo, pero un enorme malestar se apodera de su cuerpecito, y acaba pinchándola sin querer. Una historia entrañable con la que ayudar a tu peque a detectar y comunicar mejor sus sentimientos.

Muy atentos: Después de casi dos años de desarrollo, por fin llega TCA ConvertDoc 1.5. No es una simple actualización: es un salto generacional con las funcionalidades que me habéis ido pidiendo en los comentarios del blog, sobre todo desde la entrada de la versión 1.4. Para quienes aún no lo conozcan: ¿Qué es TCA ConvertDoc? TCA ConvertDoc es una pequeña utilidad portable y gratuita para Windows, con interfaz 100% accesible y atajos de teclado, que nos permite convertir entre multitud de formatos de documentos (doc, docx, RTF, epub, pdf, HTML, odt, txt, markdown, PNG, JPG, PPTx), hacer OCR a imágenes y PDFs, y ahora, además, traducir. Y todo, de forma individual o por lotes (carpeta entera de una sola vez). Pues bien, la 1.5 llega cargada de novedades. Os las cuento todas. Novedades de TCA ConvertDoc 1.5 1. Conversión DOCX → PDF (individual y por lotes) Ahora podéis convertir documentos de Word a PDF con un solo clic. ¿Tenéis una carpeta llena de? docx? La conversión masiva procesa todo el directorio de golpe, manteniendo el formato, las imágenes y la estructura del documento. Perfecto para preparar entregas, archivar o compartir. 2. Conversión PPTX → Markdown (individual y por lotes) Algunos me preguntasteis en la entrada de la 1.4 por qué ciertas presentaciones de PowerPoint no se pueden leer con lectores de pantalla. Pues esta es una de las soluciones: extrae el contenido de tus presentaciones a Markdown limpio y editable, ideal para documentación, blogs, wikis o migrar contenido. También funciona en lote para carpetas completas. 3. PDF escaneado PDF buscable (OCR) "¿Se puede convertir un pdf en un pdf con capacidad de búsqueda?" — me preguntasteis en los comentarios de la 1.4. ¡Ahora sí! Añades un PDF que es solo imagen (un escaneo sin capa de texto), TCA ConvertDoc le aplica OCR y te devuelve un PDF con texto seleccionable y buscable. Accesibilidad real para documentos heredados, del tipo que sea. 4. JPG / PNG PDF buscable Construye PDFs accesibles a partir de imágenes sueltas. Cada imagen pasa por OCR y se une en un único PDF donde puedes buscar, copiar y seleccionar el texto. Ideal para digitalizar notas, facturas, páginas de libros o documentos fotografiados con el móvil. 5. Traducción integrada! (¡la gran novedad!) Llevaba muchísimo tiempo queriendo incorporarle la traducción a TCA ConvertDoc, y por fin está aquí. Ahora el programa es capaz de traducir archivos completos a cualquier idioma usando dos motores: • Argos Translate | Offline | Descarga previa de los paquetes de idioma (privacidad total, sin internet) • Google Translate | Online | Conexión a internet, máxima calidad Formatos soportados: .txt, .docx y .pdf. Y lo mejor de todo: traduce incluso archivos grandes como libros enteros. El motor procesa el texto en fragmentos inteligentes, mantiene la estructura del documento (párrafos, saltos de página, estilos en DOCX) y te entrega el archivo traducido listo para usar. Nada de copiar y pegar por trozos, ni de chocar con límites ridículos de caracteres. Un detalle importante sobre Argos: la primera vez que uses Argos con un idioma, te aparecerá un diálogo ofreciéndote descargar los paquetes de ese idioma... y solo esa única vez. A partir de ahí, ese idioma queda instalado en el programa y funciona totalmente sin conexión. Tranquilo, no te lo volverá a pedir. 6. Selector de idiomas del OCR (Tesseract) completo En la 1.4 teníamos 3 idiomas de OCR (español, inglés e italiano). Ahora, en el cuadro combinado de idioma del OCR aparecen todos los idiomas que soporta Tesseract. Ya no hay que editar configs a mano ni adivinar códigos: eliges el idioma y listo. 7. Arreglos y optimizaciones internas OCR de archivos grandes: se ha reescrito el proceso para manejar PDFs e imágenes de gran tamaño sin agotar la memoria ni bloquear la interfaz. Gestión de hilos optimizada en las conversiones por lotes. Mejor detección de orientación y enderezado automático en imágenes escaneadas. Logs más claros y barra de progreso real en las operaciones largas. Y muchas otras mejoras internas que hacen el programa más estable y rápido. Requisitos para utilizar TCA ConvertDoc 1.5: • Windows10 (x64) en adelante. • portable, sin instalación. • Para Argos: el programa te ofrece descargar los paquetes del idioma la primera vez que lo uses (un solo diálogo), y luego funciona offline • Para Google Translate: conexión a internet Tip: si vas a trabajar mucho con traducción offline, entra a Argos, descarga de una vez los idiomas que más uses (español, inglés, francés, alemán, chino, japonés, árabe...) y olvídate. Luego todo irá 100% sin conexión. Tutorial: 📘 TCA ConvertDoc 1.5: OCR en PDF, 🚀 traduce libros y más! En este tutorial les mostraré: • Les mostraré la nueva conversión de Docx a PDF. • Conversión de PPTX a Markdown. • Conversión de un PDF (que son imágenes) a un PDF accesible (que admite búsqueda). • Construir un archivo PDF a partir de imágenes Jpg o PNG. • Muestra de que todos los idiomas ahora se cargan en el Motor OCR Tesseract. • Como traducir un documento en formato TXT a otro idioma de forma Online usando Google Translate (• conversión del inglés al español). • Como traducir un documento en formato Docx, utilizando la traducción OfLine con Argos Translate (• muestra del inglés al francés, descarga de idiomas y más). • Finalmente les mostraré, como traducir un PDF a otro idioma. La descarga. Les dejaré en la descarga: • El audio tutorial (en los canales Odysse y YouTube estará en video tutorial). • El programa TCA ConvertDoc 1.5 x64. • Archivo con las librerías visual estudio C++. Espero les sea de mucha utilidad: Dos años son mucho tiempo en software, pero TCA ConvertDoc 1.5 llega para quedarse. No es un parche: es un salto que cubre el ciclo completo —convertir, OCR, buscar, traducir— en una sola herramienta accesible, portable, gratuita y sin suscripciones. Si trabajas con documentos, investigas, digitalizas archivo o necesitas mover contenido entre idiomas, esta versión te va a ahorrar horas. Y la traducción de libros enteros, esa que tanto esperabais, por fin es una realidad. ¿Qué funcionalidad echabas más en falta? ¿Se te ocurre algo para la 1?6? en.summary: We’re so close to 2026.2 now! We have a release candidate! Plus, this time around: NVDA 2026.2 Release Candidate! Automatically Scrolling the Braille Display Getting help from others New Unassigned Commands Finding out more about what is new NVDA 2026.2 Release Candidate! The NVDA 2026.2 Release Candidate is now available for testing! We encourage all… Read More
en.body:
We’re so close to 2026.2 now! We have a release candidate! Plus, this time around:

The NVDA 2026.2 Release Candidate is now available for testing! We encourage all users to download this RC and provide feedback. Unless any critical bugs are found, this will be identical to the final 2026.2 release.

NVDA 2026.2 includes:

Magnifier (full screen, colour filtering, zoom, focus tracking) Improved touch gestures (links, form fields, etc) NVDA+x to repeat last spoken information Improved speech dictionaries Automatic Braille Display scrolling & much more!

We would encourage you to try out the NVDA 2026.2 Release Candidate , especially if you haven’t yet tried any of the betas. You can do this by creating a portable copy or by selecting “Continue running” from the launcher, to run a temporary copy and not interfere with your installed copy of NVDA.

One of the new features in NVDA 2026.2, is that we: “Added the ability to automatically scroll the braille display”. This comes courtesy of Noelia, one of our prominent Spanish contributors. Reading the user guide entry for the new “Automatic scroll rate” feature, it notes:

Automatic braille scrolling can be enabled to scroll the display at a set speed. When using this feature, the braille display scrolls to present information which is more than will fit on the display at once. The feature is disabled by default. You can change the gestures assigned to use automatic braille scrolling in NVDA’s Input Gestures dialog before it can be used. Gestures are also available to speed up or slow down the rate of automatic scrolling. Alternatively, you can set the automatic scroll rate in Braille Settings.

While braille is scrolling, you can still use the scroll back and scroll forward commands without stopping scrolling. Scroll back can be useful to read previous contents again. Scroll forward can be useful to skip a blank line, or if the line being read is short.

While reading, automatic braille scrolling will stop when any of the following happen:

The toggle automatic braille scrolling key is pressed The user presses a key or gesture which would display a new message The focus is moved (including with braille display panning keys) The end of the document is reached The state of the lock or secure screen is changed (such as the computer being locked)

The commands for this feature are: Toggle automatic scroll: NVDA+alt+k Increase automatic scroll: NVDA+alt+L Decrease automatic scroll: NVDA+alt+j

Last fortnight, we covered ways you can get help from within NVDA itself. This time around, let’s have a look at some of the places you can get help from others. As with last fortnight’s post, this list covers getting help for NVDA itself only, aimed at end users: NV Access Telephone Support : If you’ve still got questions after following last fortnight’s tips and reading Basic Training for NVDA etc, give us a call. Telephone support IS a paid service, and for end-user support only, but it is available 24/7. We have numbers you can call in Australia or the USA, OR you can email us and we can call you anywhere in the world. You also get telephone support included with the NVDA Productivity Bundle . Official NVDA Email Group : While we monitor various other groups, the one place you know you will find NV Access staff, and users, is the official, friendly, NVDA email group at https://nvaccess.org/nvda-users – plus, as a free, welcoming and popular resource, you will often get help from other users even quicker than we can respond. Local language email groups : We have a huge list of email groups in many languages. Know of a group which isn’t listed? Please, let us know so we can share it on the connect page for others! Social media : Our community on Mastodon is the most active, but you can also find us on Facebook and other platforms . NVDA Remote Access : Have a friend who can help with your PC? You can let them connect to your PC to help you. Note there are a number of security measures in place to ensure this feature can only be accessed by deliberate action from both parties.

For the upcoming NVDA 2026.2, we’ve added a couple of new “unassigned” commands. These aren’t always the most obvious to find, so I thought it was worth highlighting them here: Added an unassigned command to toggle keyboard layout. ( #19211 , @CyrilleB79 ) Added an unassigned Quick Navigation Command for jumping to next/previous slider in browse mode. ( #17005 , @tareh7z ) Added an unassigned command to report the current status of the Screen Curtain. ( #19759 )

Commands like these can provide useful functionality, but may often only be required by some users. As we are all aware, screen readers already have a lot of keystrokes, so we always have to think carefully before assigning new keystrokes.

For instance, the toggle keyboard layout setting. Most users will setup the keyboard layout how they prefer, and never need to change it. For the rare time you may wish to change it, the setting is on the keyboard settings page, which is available with NVDA+control+k . For testing or teaching, a command to toggle the layout on the fly may be invaluable, so, in NVDA 2026.2, it’s there if you need it.

In any NVDA release announcement , there is a link to “ What’s new in this release of NVDA ” (I’ve linked to those to things for NVDA 2026.2 RC1). That document gives a summary of the highlights in several paragraphs, and then bullet points for all the changes in groups: Important notes : information such as older Windows versions no longer supported Security fixes : Updates to NVDA which fix potential security issues. New features : New functionality in NVDA. For instance, NVDA+x to repeat the last spoken information, or the ability to automatically scroll the braille display Changes : Features which may be slightly different, such as renaming the “COM Registration Fixing Tool” to “System Accessibility Repair Tool”. Bug fixes : Fixing features which didn’t work the way they should. For instance, in NVDA 2026.2, we’ve fixed a crash in the add-on store, NVDA now recovers quicker from freezes in some applications, and form controls are correctly reported in Firefox again. Changes for developers : Updates which may affect how contributors code for NVDA. These don’t affect end users directly. For instance, updating the version of Python used, or new functions developers can call to find out information. Deprecations : Again, only for developers, function calls which either no longer work, or have been changed to something else, and developers should transition over to the new function call.

In most of the bullet points for each release, there is a number at the end, and sometimes a username. For instance, in the unassigned commands article above: “Added an unassigned Quick Navigation Command for jumping to next/previous slider in browse mode. ( #17005 , @tareh7z )”

In this case, #17005 is the issue number assigned to the original request for this feature. @tareh7z is the GitHub user who wrote the code and submitted the pull request to fix it – thanks @tareh7z! And thanks to ALL our contributors. NVDA 2026.2 is a big release with a lot of amazing features the community have put a lot of work into!

The line in the changes document will hopefully give enough information to quickly describe the feature for most users. The user guide will also have been updated with any relevant information. In this case, look at section 6.1.3 “Other Navigation Commands”, which talks about not only sliders, but other quick navigation commands which don’t have default keystrokes.

The issue number is a link back to that issue, which can be helpful if you’d like to look back at the conversation which prompted the new feature. For instance, in this case, there was some discussion around what other types of information could potentially be accessed with a “slider” command (others that were suggested were ruled out in this case).

That’s all for this time. Do please try out the NVDA 2026.2 release candidate , and of course, let us know of any issues you encounter with it. Next time around we will have more on NVDA 2026.2!
